subject: tourism
description: Tourism question bank, FET Grade 10 (CAPS FET Tourism Grades 10-12). Keyed by atomic skill id. Each skill holds a ~20-item pool; mastery = 60% (FET, no timer). All input types tap-based (no free-text). Mirrors data/history-question-bank.json schema. Authored as proof for head-of-ed review.

TOUR.G10.T1.INTRO.A1.title: Introduction to tourism
TOUR.G10.T1.INTRO.A1.description: What tourism is; the difference between inbound and outbound tourism; the concepts domestic, regional and international tourism; what a tourist is; why people travel; and tourists' needs, preferences and expectations.
TOUR.G10.T1.INTRO.A1.recovery_strategy: Anchor on the traveller's home country and direction of travel: inbound = into SA from abroad; outbound = SA residents going abroad; domestic = travel inside one's own country.

questions.question: What does the word 'tourism' describe?
options: Travelling away from your usual home environment for leisure, business or other reasons, staying at least one night but less than a year
Only travelling overseas for a holiday
Moving permanently to live in another country
Travelling to work and back each day
questions.expected: Travelling away from your usual home environment for leisure, business or other reasons, staying at least one night but less than a year
questions.memo: Tourism is travel away from your usual environment for a limited time (under a year) for any purpose — leisure, business, visiting family, health and more. Moving permanently is migration, not tourism.

questions.question: What is inbound tourism?
options: Foreign visitors travelling INTO South Africa
South Africans travelling OUT to other countries
South Africans travelling within South Africa
Goods being imported into South Africa
questions.expected: Foreign visitors travelling INTO South Africa
questions.memo: Inbound = coming IN. Inbound tourists are foreigners arriving in South Africa. Think of the direction of travel relative to the country.

questions.question: A South African citizen flies to Thailand for a holiday. This is an example of:
questions.memo: Outbound = going OUT of your own country. A South African leaving for Thailand is an outbound tourist from South Africa's point of view.

questions.question: True or false: A family from Johannesburg spending a week in Durban are inbound tourists.
questions.memo: They are travelling WITHIN their own country, so they are domestic tourists. Inbound tourists come into the country from abroad.

questions.question: Travel by residents within their own country is called _________ tourism.
questions.memo: Domestic tourism happens inside one's own country — for example a Capetonian visiting the Kruger National Park.

questions.question: A South African travels to Botswana, a neighbouring SADC country. This is best described as:
questions.memo: Regional tourism is travel within the same region — for South Africa that means the SADC countries close to home, such as Botswana, Namibia or Zimbabwe.

questions.question: What is international tourism?
options: Travel that crosses an international border between countries
Travel only within your home province
Travel that never involves an aeroplane
Travel that lasts longer than one year
questions.expected: Travel that crosses an international border between countries
questions.memo: International tourism involves crossing a border from one country into another. It includes both inbound and outbound travel.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a tourist?
options: Someone who travels away from their usual environment and stays at least one night, but less than a year
Anyone who leaves their house for any reason
Only a person on an overseas holiday
Someone who has moved to a new town permanently
questions.expected: Someone who travels away from their usual environment and stays at least one night, but less than a year
questions.memo: A tourist travels away from home and stays overnight, but not permanently. The trip is temporary.

questions.question: True or false: A person travelling for business cannot be counted as a tourist.
questions.memo: Business is one of the recognised reasons people travel. A business traveller who stays away overnight is a tourist.

questions.question: Which of these is a common reason people travel?
options: To avoid ever seeing new places
To stop needing food and rest
questions.memo: People travel for many reasons: leisure, business, visiting friends and relatives (VFR), health, religion, sport, study and more.

questions.question: Sort each traveller into the correct type of tourism.

items.text: A tourist from France visiting Table Mountain
A Durban couple touring the Garden Route
A Pretoria student flying to study in Australia
A German tour group arriving at OR Tambo
A Gauteng family driving to the Kruger Park
A South African businessperson flying to London

questions.memo: Inbound = foreigners coming into SA; outbound = South Africans going abroad; domestic = travel within SA. Always look at the home country and the direction of travel.

questions.question: A tourist from Germany visiting Cape Town is, to South Africa, an _________ tourist.
questions.memo: From South Africa's point of view, a foreign visitor coming in is an inbound tourist.

questions.question: Why is it useful for a tourism business to understand a tourist's needs, preferences and expectations?
options: So it can offer products and service that satisfy the tourist
So it can charge every tourist exactly the same price
So it can avoid ever changing its products
So it can ignore what tourists actually want
questions.expected: So it can offer products and service that satisfy the tourist
questions.memo: Knowing what tourists need and expect lets a business meet those expectations, which leads to satisfied customers and repeat business.

questions.question: True or false: All tourists have exactly the same needs and expectations.
questions.memo: Different tourists want different things. A backpacker and a luxury traveller have very different needs, preferences and expectations.

questions.question: A South African resident going to study for a year in Canada is an example of:
questions.memo: Leaving South Africa to travel to another country is outbound tourism, even when the purpose is study.

questions.question: Travel to a neighbouring SADC country such as Namibia is an example of _________ tourism.
questions.memo: Regional tourism is travel within the same region — for South Africa, the SADC countries.

questions.question: Which of the following is an EXPECTATION a tourist might reasonably have of a guesthouse?
options: A clean, safe room and friendly service
Permanent residence with no checkout date
questions.expected: A clean, safe room and friendly service
questions.memo: Expectations are the reasonable standards a tourist hopes for, such as cleanliness, safety, comfort and good service.

questions.question: True or false: Domestic tourism helps keep tourists' spending inside South Africa's economy.
questions.memo: When South Africans holiday at home, their money stays in the local economy, supporting South African businesses and jobs.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the term to its meaning?
options: Inbound = into the country; Outbound = out of the country
Inbound = out of the country; Outbound = into the country
Inbound = within a province; Outbound = within a city
Inbound = by sea only; Outbound = by air only
questions.expected: Inbound = into the country; Outbound = out of the country
questions.memo: Keep the direction clear: IN-bound comes in, OUT-bound goes out.

questions.question: Sort each example as a NEED or a PREFERENCE for a traveller.

items.text: A sea-view room rather than a garden-view room
A particular brand of coffee at breakfast

questions.memo: A need is something a traveller must have (water, food, shelter, safety). A preference is something they would like but can do without.

TOUR.G10.T1.TYPES.A1.title: Types of tourists & tourist profiles
TOUR.G10.T1.TYPES.A1.description: Recognising types of tourists (VFR, leisure, adventure, business, shopping, health, eco, cultural, religious, sport & recreation, education, special interest, incentive, backpacker/youth, gap year) and drawing up a tourist profile linking needs and preferences.
TOUR.G10.T1.TYPES.A1.recovery_strategy: Identify the main PURPOSE of the trip first — that purpose names the tourist type (visiting family = VFR; nature with low impact = eco; reward trip paid by employer = incentive).

questions.question: What does the tourist type 'VFR' stand for?
questions.memo: VFR tourists travel mainly to spend time with friends and family. It is one of the most common reasons people travel.

questions.question: Which description best fits an eco-tourist?
options: A traveller who visits natural areas responsibly, with low impact on the environment
A traveller who only stays in five-star city hotels
A traveller whose main goal is shopping in malls
questions.expected: A traveller who visits natural areas responsibly, with low impact on the environment
questions.memo: Eco-tourists value nature and want their visit to harm the environment as little as possible.

questions.question: A tourist who travels mainly to do thrilling activities like white-water rafting and bungee jumping is best described as a(n):
questions.memo: Adventure tourists seek excitement and physical challenge through activities such as rafting, hiking and bungee jumping.

questions.question: An employee wins a free trip from her company as a reward for top sales. What type of tourist is she?
questions.memo: Incentive travel is a reward given by an employer to motivate or thank staff. The company pays for the trip.

questions.question: Which tourist type travels mainly to attend meetings, conferences or trade fairs?
questions.memo: Business tourists travel for work reasons such as meetings, conferences, exhibitions and trade fairs.

questions.question: A tourist who travels to another country for a medical procedure or to recover at a spa is a:
questions.memo: Health tourists travel to improve their health or wellbeing — for treatment, surgery, or rest and relaxation at wellness centres.

questions.question: A traveller who visits museums, festivals and historic sites to experience a region's way of life is a:
questions.memo: Cultural tourists travel to experience the customs, history, art and heritage of a place.

questions.question: A 'special interest tourist' (SIT) is best described as someone who:
options: Travels to pursue a specific hobby or interest, such as bird-watching or photography
Travels only for general sightseeing with no particular focus
Never plans their trip in advance
questions.expected: Travels to pursue a specific hobby or interest, such as bird-watching or photography
questions.memo: Special interest tourists build their trip around one focused interest — for example wine, birding, photography or trains.

questions.question: True or false: Backpackers usually travel on a tight budget and often stay away for longer periods.
questions.memo: Backpacker / youth travellers typically keep costs low, stay in hostels and travel for extended periods.

questions.question: True or false: A gap-year traveller is someone taking a single weekend break.
questions.memo: A gap year is an extended break (often around a year), typically taken between school and further study or work, used to travel and gain experience.

questions.question: VFR stands for visiting friends and _________.
questions.memo: VFR = Visiting Friends and Relatives.

questions.question: A tourist whose main aim is to relax on a beach and unwind is a _________ tourist.
questions.memo: Leisure tourists travel mainly to relax and enjoy themselves on holiday.

questions.question: What is a tourist profile?
options: A description of a type of tourist, including their needs, preferences and travel behaviour
A photograph taken at a tourist attraction
A map showing where a tourist has travelled
The price a tourist pays for a tour package
questions.expected: A description of a type of tourist, including their needs, preferences and travel behaviour
questions.memo: A tourist profile sums up who a tourist is and what they want, helping businesses plan suitable products and services.

questions.question: Why would a tour operator draw up a tourist profile before designing a package?
options: To match the products and services to what that type of tourist needs and prefers
To make the package as expensive as possible
To make sure every tourist gets exactly the same trip
To avoid having to advertise the package
questions.expected: To match the products and services to what that type of tourist needs and prefers
questions.memo: A profile guides the business to offer the right accommodation, activities and price for that tourist, improving satisfaction and sales.

questions.question: Sort each traveller into the correct tourist type.

items.text: Goes shark-cage diving and abseiling on holiday
Flies to a two-day company conference
Travels to spend December with her grandparents
Attends a trade exhibition to meet suppliers
Books a multi-day hiking and rafting trip
Visits an old school friend in another city

questions.memo: Identify the main purpose: thrill-seeking = adventure; work = business; seeing family or friends = VFR.

questions.question: A tourist who travels to take part in a pilgrimage to a holy site is a:
questions.memo: Religious tourists travel for faith reasons, such as pilgrimages, festivals or visits to sacred places.

questions.question: A group travelling to watch the Comrades Marathon are mainly:
questions.memo: Sport and recreation tourists travel to take part in or watch sporting events.

questions.question: True or false: Incentive travel is normally paid for by the tourists themselves.
questions.memo: Incentive trips are paid for by an employer or company as a reward, not by the traveller.

questions.question: A learner travelling abroad on a school exchange to attend classes is a(n) _________ tourist.
questions.memo: Education tourists travel mainly to learn or study — for example school tours, exchanges or courses.

questions.question: Match each tourist profile to the holiday it would most likely prefer.

items.text: A five-star hotel with spa treatments
A shared dormitory in a budget hostel
Private guided tours and fine dining
A long, flexible trip with low daily costs

questions.memo: Match preferences to the profile: luxury tourists value comfort and exclusivity and will pay for it; backpackers value low cost and flexibility.

TOUR.G10.T1.TRANSPORT.A1.title: Modes of transport
TOUR.G10.T1.TRANSPORT.A1.description: Road, air, rail, water and extraordinary modes with examples; comparing them on comfort, cost, safety, carrying capacity, speed and reliability; advantages and disadvantages of each.
TOUR.G10.T1.TRANSPORT.A1.recovery_strategy: Sort by the surface the vehicle moves on: road (car/bus/taxi), rail (train/tram), air (plane/helicopter), water (cruise/yacht), extraordinary (camel/balloon).

questions.question: Which of these is a ROAD mode of transport?
questions.memo: Road transport moves on roads: cars, buses, coaches, shuttles, metered and minibus taxis, and motorcycles.

questions.question: Which of these is an AIR mode of transport?
questions.memo: Air transport includes aeroplanes, helicopters and microlights.

questions.question: Which of these is a RAIL mode of transport?
questions.memo: Rail transport runs on tracks: trains and trams.

questions.question: Which of these is a WATER mode of transport?
questions.memo: Water transport includes luxury cruise liners, chartered boats and yachts.

questions.question: Which of these is an EXTRAORDINARY mode of transport?
questions.memo: Extraordinary modes are unusual ones used for the experience: camels, donkey carts, hot air balloons and bicycles.

questions.question: Sort each example into the correct mode of transport.
questions.memo: Group by the surface the vehicle uses: road, rail (tracks), air or water.

questions.question: True or false: A minibus taxi is a road mode of transport.
questions.memo: Minibus taxis travel on roads, so they are a road mode of transport.

questions.question: For moving the largest number of passengers at once on a single ocean voyage, which mode has the greatest carrying capacity?
questions.memo: Carrying capacity is how many passengers can travel at once. A cruise liner can carry thousands; a taxi or microlight only a few.

questions.question: Which mode of transport is usually the FASTEST over a very long distance (for example, Johannesburg to London)?
questions.memo: Over long distances, air travel is by far the fastest mode.

questions.question: True or false: Flying is almost always the cheapest option for a family of five travelling 300 km within a province.
questions.memo: For short distances, road travel by car is usually cheaper for a family than buying five air tickets.

questions.question: Which is an ADVANTAGE of road transport for a tourist?
options: It is flexible and can take you door-to-door
It is always faster than flying
It never gets stuck in traffic
questions.expected: It is flexible and can take you door-to-door
questions.memo: Road transport is flexible: you can stop where you like and travel from your door right to the destination.

questions.question: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of road transport over a very long trip?
options: It can be slow and tiring, with traffic and many stops
It can never reach small towns
It always costs more than flying
questions.expected: It can be slow and tiring, with traffic and many stops
questions.memo: Over long distances road travel takes much longer than flying and can be tiring, with delays from traffic.

questions.question: Which is an ADVANTAGE of rail travel for tourists?
options: It can carry many passengers comfortably and offer scenic views
It can travel anywhere without tracks
It is always the cheapest option
questions.expected: It can carry many passengers comfortably and offer scenic views
questions.memo: Trains move many people at once in comfort and often pass through scenic landscapes — a draw for tourists.

questions.question: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of air travel?
options: It is usually expensive and needs time for check-in and security
It is the slowest way to cross long distances
It can only carry one passenger
questions.expected: It is usually expensive and needs time for check-in and security
questions.memo: Air travel is fast but costly, and passengers must arrive early for check-in, security and boarding.

questions.question: Travel by ship, such as a luxury cruise liner, is a _________ mode of transport.
questions.memo: Ships and boats travel on water.

questions.question: A helicopter is an example of _________ transport.
questions.memo: Helicopters fly, so they are an air mode of transport.

questions.question: Place these modes in order from SLOWEST to FASTEST for a long cross-country journey.
questions.memo: Typical speed rises from a bicycle, to a bus on the road, to a high-speed train, to an aeroplane (the fastest over long distances).

questions.question: When we compare transport modes, 'reliability' means:
options: How dependable the service is at running on time
How many bags it can carry
questions.expected: How dependable the service is at running on time
questions.memo: Reliability is about whether the transport runs on schedule and can be depended upon.

questions.question: On a long trip, which mode would usually offer the MOST comfort and personal space?
questions.memo: Comfort compares how pleasant the journey is. A luxury cruise liner offers cabins, restaurants and space, far more comfort than a crowded taxi or a motorcycle.

questions.question: Sort each statement about AIR travel as an advantage or a disadvantage.

items.text: Fastest way to cover long distances
Can reach far-away international destinations quickly
Long check-in, security and boarding times

questions.memo: Air travel's speed and reach are advantages; its high cost and the time spent on airport procedures and luggage limits are disadvantages.

TOUR.G10.T1.ACCOM.A1.title: Accommodation establishments — types, facilities & services
TOUR.G10.T1.ACCOM.A1.description: Formal-service, guest, self-catering, caravan/camping and backpacker accommodation; the difference between a facility (what the tourist can use) and a service (what the establishment does for the tourist).
TOUR.G10.T1.ACCOM.A1.recovery_strategy: A facility is a THING the guest uses (pool, gym, gift shop). A service is an ACTION staff perform (laundry, guided walk, shuttle).

questions.question: Which of these is a FORMAL-SERVICE accommodation establishment?
questions.memo: Formal-service accommodation (hotels, lodges and game lodges) provides full service, including meals and housekeeping.

questions.question: A bed-and-breakfast (B&B) is an example of which category?
questions.memo: Guest accommodation includes country houses, guest houses and B&Bs — smaller, more personal places to stay.

questions.question: Which of these is SELF-CATERING accommodation?
options: A holiday chalet with its own kitchen
questions.expected: A holiday chalet with its own kitchen
questions.memo: Self-catering accommodation (chalets, cottages, apartments) gives guests a kitchen so they can prepare their own meals.

questions.question: Which type of accommodation is aimed mainly at budget youth travellers?
questions.memo: Backpacker accommodation and hostels offer low-cost, often shared, accommodation popular with young travellers.

questions.question: A caravan and camping establishment is best described as:
options: A site where guests stay in caravans or tents, often with shared facilities
A five-star hotel with room service
A type of guest house with private suites
questions.expected: A site where guests stay in caravans or tents, often with shared facilities
questions.memo: Caravan and camping sites provide stands for caravans or tents, usually with shared ablutions and other facilities.

questions.question: Which of these is a FACILITY at an accommodation establishment?
questions.memo: A facility is something the guest can use (pool, gym, gift shop). The others listed are services — actions staff perform.

questions.question: Which of these is a SERVICE offered to guests?
questions.memo: A service is an action staff perform for the guest, such as laundry, a guided walk or a shuttle. The others are facilities.

questions.question: True or false: A bed-and-breakfast is a type of formal-service hotel.
questions.memo: A B&B is guest accommodation, not formal-service. Hotels, lodges and game lodges are the formal-service category.

questions.question: True or false: Self-catering accommodation means guests can prepare their own meals.
questions.memo: Self-catering means 'catering for yourself' — the unit has a kitchen so guests cook for themselves.

questions.question: Accommodation where guests cook their own meals is called _________-catering.
questions.memo: Self-catering = guests cater (cook and cater) for themselves.

questions.question: Sort each establishment into the correct accommodation category.

items.text: A self-contained apartment with a kitchen
A guest house run by a family

questions.memo: Formal-service = hotels and lodges; guest = guest houses and B&Bs; self-catering = units with kitchens; backpacker = budget hostels.

questions.question: Sort each item as a FACILITY or a SERVICE.
questions.memo: If guests USE it themselves it is a facility; if STAFF do it for them it is a service.

questions.question: A luxury game lodge in a private reserve falls under which accommodation category?
questions.memo: Game lodges, like hotels, provide full formal service including meals and housekeeping.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a guest house?
options: A smaller, more personal establishment offering rooms and usually some meals
A large hotel chain with hundreds of rooms
A campsite for tents and caravans
questions.expected: A smaller, more personal establishment offering rooms and usually some meals
questions.memo: Guest houses are smaller and more home-like than hotels, offering personal service.

questions.question: A shared, low-cost place to stay that is popular with young travellers is a _________.
questions.memo: Hostels offer budget, often shared, accommodation for backpackers and youth travellers.

questions.question: True or false: A gymnasium provided at a hotel is best classified as a service.
questions.memo: A gymnasium is a facility — something guests use. A service is an action staff perform.

questions.question: Which definition best describes a 'facility'?
options: Something the tourist can make use of, such as a pool or gym
An action staff perform for the tourist, such as laundry
The star rating of the establishment
questions.expected: Something the tourist can make use of, such as a pool or gym
questions.memo: Facilities are things provided for guests to use.

questions.question: Which definition best describes a 'service'?
options: Something the establishment does for the tourist, such as a shuttle or laundry
A physical thing guests use, such as a swimming pool
questions.expected: Something the establishment does for the tourist, such as a shuttle or laundry
questions.memo: Services are actions staff perform for guests.

questions.question: A family on a tight budget wants to cook their own meals and stay near the beach. Which accommodation suits them best?
questions.memo: Self-catering lets the family cook for themselves, which keeps costs down — a good match for their needs.

questions.question: Match each tourist to the most suitable accommodation.

items.text: A business traveller wanting room service and a gym
A young traveller on a tight budget
A family touring with their own caravan
A guest who wants daily housekeeping and a concierge
A backpacker happy to share a dormitory

questions.memo: Match the tourist's budget and needs to the accommodation: full service for those who will pay for comfort; hostels for budget travellers; caravan parks for self-drive campers.

TOUR.G10.T1.GRADING.A1.title: The South African grading system
TOUR.G10.T1.GRADING.A1.description: The star grading system; the role of the Tourism Grading Council of South Africa (TGCSA); the benefits of grading for tourists and establishments; the procedure to be graded; logos displayed on grading.
TOUR.G10.T1.GRADING.A1.recovery_strategy: Grading in SA is VOLUNTARY and awarded by an independent body (TGCSA), not by the establishment. More stars = higher quality of facilities and service.

questions.question: What does TGCSA stand for?
options: Tourism Grading Council of South Africa
Tourist Guide Course of South Africa
Travel and Geography Centre of South Africa
Tourism Growth Committee of South Africa
questions.expected: Tourism Grading Council of South Africa
questions.memo: The TGCSA is the official, independent body that awards star grading to accommodation and venues in South Africa.

questions.question: What does the star grading of an establishment mainly measure?
options: The quality of its facilities and service
How close it is to an airport
questions.expected: The quality of its facilities and service
questions.memo: Stars reflect quality. More stars mean a higher standard of facilities and service, not just size or age.

questions.question: True or false: Star grading in South Africa is compulsory for every accommodation establishment.
questions.memo: Grading is VOLUNTARY in South Africa. Establishments choose whether to apply to the TGCSA.

questions.question: True or false: An establishment decides for itself how many stars to display.
questions.memo: An independent body, the TGCSA, assesses and awards the stars — not the establishment itself.

questions.question: Who awards the star grading to a South African establishment?
options: The Tourism Grading Council of South Africa (TGCSA)
questions.expected: The Tourism Grading Council of South Africa (TGCSA)
questions.memo: The TGCSA is the independent authority that grades establishments.

questions.question: In the South African system, more stars generally mean:
options: A higher quality of facilities and service
questions.expected: A higher quality of facilities and service
questions.memo: The grading runs from 1 to 5 stars; the more stars, the higher the standard.

questions.question: What is a benefit of grading FOR THE TOURIST?
options: It gives a reliable indication of the quality they can expect
It guarantees the cheapest possible price
It means they never have to book in advance
It removes the need to read reviews ever again
questions.expected: It gives a reliable indication of the quality they can expect
questions.memo: Grading helps tourists know what standard to expect before they book, making choices easier and more reliable.

questions.question: What is a benefit of grading FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT?
options: It is a marketing advantage that builds credibility and attracts guests
It forces the business to lower all its prices
It removes the need to maintain standards
It bans competitors from the area
questions.expected: It is a marketing advantage that builds credibility and attracts guests
questions.memo: A recognised grade is a trusted marketing tool — it reassures guests and helps the business compete.

questions.question: The South African star grading runs from 1 star up to _________ stars.
questions.memo: The scale is 1 to 5 stars, with 5 being the highest quality.

questions.question: True or false: A successfully graded establishment may display the official TGCSA logo and star plaque.
questions.memo: Once graded, an establishment may display its star plaque and the TGCSA logo to show its official rating.

questions.question: What is the correct first step for an establishment that wants to be graded?
options: Apply to the TGCSA, which then assesses the establishment
Ask its guests to vote on a rating
Wait for the government to inspect it without applying
questions.expected: Apply to the TGCSA, which then assesses the establishment
questions.memo: The establishment applies to the TGCSA; an assessor then evaluates it against the grading criteria before a grade is awarded.

questions.question: Compared with a 3-star establishment, a 5-star establishment is expected to offer:
options: A higher standard of facilities and more extensive service
Exactly the same standard at a lower price
Fewer services but a better view
questions.expected: A higher standard of facilities and more extensive service
questions.memo: Higher grades require higher standards — 5-star establishments offer superior facilities and a wider range of quality services.

questions.question: Sort each benefit by who it mainly helps.

items.text: Knows what quality to expect before booking
Can market itself with a trusted star rating
Gains credibility that attracts more guests
Feels more confident the place is reliable

questions.memo: For tourists, grading guides and reassures their choice; for establishments, it is a credibility and marketing advantage.

questions.question: Why might a tourist feel more confident booking a graded hotel rather than an ungraded one?
options: The grade is awarded by an independent body, so the quality has been checked
Graded hotels never need to be booked
questions.expected: The grade is awarded by an independent body, so the quality has been checked
questions.memo: Because an independent assessor checks the establishment, the grade is a trustworthy signal of quality.

questions.question: The body responsible for grading is the Tourism _________ Council of South Africa.
questions.memo: TGCSA = Tourism Grading Council of South Africa.

questions.question: True or false: A national grading system helps keep quality standards consistent across the industry.
questions.memo: A single national standard means a 4-star rating should mean roughly the same quality wherever you go, keeping standards consistent.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of grading?
options: It lets a poor-quality establishment claim a high rating without being checked
It helps tourists choose with confidence
It rewards establishments that maintain high standards
It builds trust in the tourism industry
questions.expected: It lets a poor-quality establishment claim a high rating without being checked
questions.memo: Grading is based on an independent assessment, so it does NOT let a poor establishment fake a high rating — that is the opposite of how it works.

questions.question: A 1-star graded establishment can be expected to offer:
options: Clean, basic, functional accommodation that meets minimum standards
questions.expected: Clean, basic, functional accommodation that meets minimum standards
questions.memo: Even the lowest grade must meet minimum standards — 1-star means clean, basic and functional, just with fewer facilities and services than higher grades.

questions.question: True or false: A higher star grade can help an establishment justify charging higher prices.
questions.memo: Higher grades signal higher quality, which lets establishments charge more — guests expect to pay for superior facilities and service.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about the South African grading system.
questions.memo: Key facts: grading is voluntary, awarded by the independent TGCSA, on a 1-to-5-star scale — it is not self-awarded and not compulsory.

TOUR.G10.T1.ACCOMTERMS.A1.title: Accommodation terminology & in-room technology
TOUR.G10.T1.ACCOMTERMS.A1.description: Concepts and abbreviations used in accommodation (twin/double/family room, suite, en suite, per person sharing, fully inclusive, B&B, a la carte, pp/pps/pppn/pppd) and in-room technology for entertainment, information, safety, comfort, work and environmental responsibility.
TOUR.G10.T1.ACCOMTERMS.A1.recovery_strategy: Break the abbreviation into parts: pp = per person, pps = per person sharing, pppn = per person per night, pppd = per person per day.

questions.question: What is a 'twin room'?
options: A room with two single beds
A room with one large double bed
A room for a family of four
Two rooms that share a bathroom
questions.expected: A room with two single beds
questions.memo: A twin room has two separate single beds, while a double room has one double bed.

questions.question: What is a 'double room'?
options: A room with one double bed for two people
A room with two single beds
A room booked for double the price
questions.expected: A room with one double bed for two people
questions.memo: A double room has a single double bed shared by two guests.

questions.question: What does 'en suite' mean?
options: The room has its own private bathroom attached
The bathroom is shared down the corridor
The room is on the top floor
questions.expected: The room has its own private bathroom attached
questions.memo: An en-suite room has a private bathroom directly connected to the bedroom.

questions.question: What does ordering 'a la carte' mean?
options: Choosing individual dishes, each separately priced, from a menu
Helping yourself from a self-service spread
Eating only the set meal of the day
questions.expected: Choosing individual dishes, each separately priced, from a menu
questions.memo: A la carte means each dish is ordered and priced separately, unlike a fixed buffet or set menu.

questions.question: What is a 'buffet'?
options: A self-service meal where guests help themselves to a variety of dishes
A single dish brought to the table
questions.expected: A self-service meal where guests help themselves to a variety of dishes
questions.memo: At a buffet, food is laid out and guests serve themselves as much as they like from the selection.

questions.question: The abbreviation 'pp' stands for per _________.
questions.memo: pp = per person.

questions.question: The abbreviation 'pps' stands for per person _________.
questions.memo: pps = per person sharing (the price each person pays when two share a room).

questions.question: What does the abbreviation 'pppn' mean?
questions.memo: pppn = per person per night — the rate one guest pays for each night.

questions.question: How does a continental breakfast differ from a full English breakfast?
options: A continental breakfast is lighter (bread, pastries, coffee); an English breakfast is cooked and hot
A continental breakfast is always larger and hot
There is no difference between them
An English breakfast contains no cooked food
questions.expected: A continental breakfast is lighter (bread, pastries, coffee); an English breakfast is cooked and hot
questions.memo: Continental = light cold items and coffee; English = a cooked hot breakfast such as eggs, bacon and sausage.

questions.question: True or false: 'Fully inclusive' means all meals are included in the price.
questions.memo: Fully inclusive (or all-inclusive) means the rate covers all meals, and often drinks and some activities too.

questions.question: What is a 'suite'?
options: A larger set of connected rooms, such as a bedroom plus a lounge
A single bed in a shared dormitory
A bathroom shared by several rooms
questions.expected: A larger set of connected rooms, such as a bedroom plus a lounge
questions.memo: A suite is more than one connected room — typically a bedroom with a separate lounge area.

questions.question: A 'family room' is best described as:
options: A larger room with extra beds to accommodate a family
A room only adults may use
questions.expected: A larger room with extra beds to accommodate a family
questions.memo: A family room has additional beds so that parents and children can share one room.

questions.question: Sort each in-room technology by its main purpose.

items.text: Electronic safe and electronic door locks
Sensors that pre-set room temperature and lighting

questions.memo: Match the technology to its purpose: locks and safes protect (safety); TV and music amuse (entertainment); temperature and towel rails make the stay pleasant (comfort).

questions.question: An electronic safe in a hotel room is in-room technology mainly for:
questions.memo: An electronic safe protects guests' valuables — its purpose is safety.

questions.question: Occupancy sensors that switch off the lights when a room is empty are mainly for:
questions.memo: Turning off lights in an empty room saves electricity, which supports environmental responsibility.

questions.question: The abbreviation 'pppd' means per person per _________.
questions.memo: pppd = per person per day.

questions.question: True or false: 'Room service' means food and drinks are brought to the guest's room.
questions.memo: Room service delivers meals and drinks directly to the guest's room.

questions.question: What is a 'penthouse'?
options: A luxurious suite on the top floor of a building
A budget room in the basement
questions.expected: A luxurious suite on the top floor of a building
questions.memo: A penthouse is a top-floor luxury suite, usually with the best views and the highest price.

questions.question: High-speed internet access and Wi-Fi in a room are in-room technology mainly for:
questions.memo: Internet access lets guests check email and work, so it supports the 'work' purpose (it also helps with information and entertainment).

questions.question: Match each abbreviation to its meaning.

items.text: The rate one guest pays each night
The price each pays when two share a room

questions.memo: pp = per person; pps = per person sharing; pppn = per person per night.

TOUR.G10.T1.FANDB.A1.title: Food & beverage establishments
TOUR.G10.T1.FANDB.A1.description: Types of food and beverage establishments: full-service restaurants (fine-dining and family), coffee shops, fast-food/quick-service, pubs/bars, dessert/ice-cream stores, taverns/shebeens, street stalls and markets.
TOUR.G10.T1.FANDB.A1.recovery_strategy: Match the establishment to its service style and speed: fine-dining = full table service; quick-service = fast, counter-based; coffee shop = light meals and drinks.

questions.question: Which best describes a fine-dining restaurant?
options: A formal restaurant with full table service and high-quality food
A counter where food is served quickly and cheaply
A stall selling snacks on the street
A shop selling only ice cream
questions.expected: A formal restaurant with full table service and high-quality food
questions.memo: Fine-dining restaurants are formal full-service restaurants offering high-quality food and attentive table service.

questions.question: Which best describes a fast-food (quick-service) establishment?
options: A place serving food quickly and cheaply, usually over a counter
A formal restaurant with waiters and a wine list
A bar that serves only alcohol
A hotel that offers room service only
questions.expected: A place serving food quickly and cheaply, usually over a counter
questions.memo: Quick-service / fast-food establishments focus on speed and low cost, with limited or no table service.

questions.question: What does a coffee shop mainly offer?
options: Coffee, other drinks and light meals
questions.expected: Coffee, other drinks and light meals
questions.memo: Coffee shops serve hot and cold drinks together with light meals and snacks.

questions.question: A pub or bar is an establishment that mainly:
options: Serves drinks, especially alcohol, often with some food
questions.expected: Serves drinks, especially alcohol, often with some food
questions.memo: Pubs and bars are beverage-focused establishments centred on serving drinks.

questions.question: A tavern or shebeen is best described as:
options: A South African establishment, often in a township, serving drinks and sometimes food
questions.expected: A South African establishment, often in a township, serving drinks and sometimes food
questions.memo: Taverns and shebeens are local South African establishments that serve drinks and often food, frequently in townships.

questions.question: What is typically sold at a street stall or street market?
options: Affordable, often local, food sold outdoors
Formal plated meals with waiter service
questions.expected: Affordable, often local, food sold outdoors
questions.memo: Street stalls and markets sell affordable food outdoors, often giving tourists a taste of local cuisine.

questions.question: True or false: A fast-food outlet offers formal fine dining with waiters serving each course.
questions.memo: Fast food is quick and counter-based; fine dining is formal with full table service. They are different categories.

questions.question: True or false: At a full-service restaurant, waiters take your order and serve you at the table.
questions.memo: Full-service restaurants (fine-dining and family restaurants) provide table service by waiters.

questions.question: An establishment serving food quickly over a counter is called a _________-food establishment.
questions.memo: Fast-food (quick-service) establishments serve food quickly, usually over a counter.

questions.question: Sort each establishment into the correct group.

items.text: A fine-dining restaurant with a wine list
A burger counter at a mall

questions.memo: Full-service = waiters serve you; quick-service = fast counter food; beverage-focused = mainly drinks (pubs, bars).

questions.question: A tourist wants a quick, cheap meal between sightseeing stops. Which establishment suits them best?
questions.memo: Quick-service outlets are best when a tourist wants food fast and cheaply.

questions.question: A couple want a special, formal dinner to celebrate an anniversary. Which suits them best?
questions.memo: A fine-dining restaurant offers the formal, high-quality experience suited to a special occasion.

questions.question: Which best describes a family restaurant?
options: A relaxed full-service restaurant suitable for families, often with a children's menu
A formal venue where children are not allowed
A bar that serves only alcohol
questions.expected: A relaxed full-service restaurant suitable for families, often with a children's menu
questions.memo: Family restaurants are full-service but informal and welcoming to children.

questions.question: A place that mainly serves coffee and light meals is a _________ shop.
questions.memo: A coffee shop serves coffee, other drinks and light meals.

questions.question: True or false: A dessert or ice-cream store specialises in sweet treats.
questions.memo: Dessert and ice-cream stores focus on sweet items such as ice cream, cakes and other desserts.

questions.question: Which of these is a BEVERAGE-focused establishment?
questions.memo: A pub focuses mainly on serving drinks, making it a beverage-focused establishment.

questions.question: Match each tourist to the most suitable food and beverage establishment.

items.text: A couple celebrating a special occasion
A traveller needing a quick, cheap bite
Someone wanting a relaxed cup of coffee and a sandwich
A foodie wanting a gourmet multi-course meal
A family grabbing burgers on the road

questions.memo: Match the occasion and budget: fine dining for special meals; fast food for speed and value; coffee shops for a casual light stop.

questions.question: What is an advantage of street food for a tourist?
options: It is affordable and offers a taste of authentic local cuisine
It is always the most formal dining option
It guarantees a private table and waiter
It is the most expensive choice
questions.expected: It is affordable and offers a taste of authentic local cuisine
questions.memo: Street food is cheap and gives tourists a genuine taste of local dishes and culture.

questions.question: True or false: Taverns and shebeens are recognised South African food and beverage establishments.
questions.memo: Taverns and shebeens are part of South Africa's food and beverage sector, serving drinks and often food.

questions.question: Which establishment offers the MOST formal level of service?
questions.memo: Fine-dining restaurants provide the most formal experience, with full table service and high-quality food.

TOUR.G10.T1.ATTRSECTOR.A1.title: The attraction sector
TOUR.G10.T1.ATTRSECTOR.A1.description: Attraction subsectors (gaming, leisure, conservation, sport & recreation, events & conferences); man-made vs natural attractions; primary vs secondary attractions; activities offered; linking an attraction to the tourist type it appeals to.
TOUR.G10.T1.ATTRSECTOR.A1.recovery_strategy: The PRIMARY attraction is the main reason for the trip; SECONDARY attractions are extras visited while there. Man-made is built by people; natural occurs in nature.

questions.question: Which of these is a MAN-MADE attraction?
questions.memo: Man-made attractions are built by people. A theme park is man-made; mountains and canyons are natural.

questions.question: Which of these is a NATURAL attraction?
questions.memo: Natural attractions occur in nature. Table Mountain is natural; museums and resorts are man-made.

questions.question: What is a PRIMARY attraction?
options: The main reason a tourist takes the trip
An extra attraction visited along the way
An attraction that is always free
The closest attraction to an airport
questions.expected: The main reason a tourist takes the trip
questions.memo: A primary attraction is the main draw — the reason the tourist travels in the first place.

questions.question: What is a SECONDARY attraction?
options: An extra attraction visited while at the destination
The main reason for the whole trip
An attraction that no tourists visit
questions.expected: An extra attraction visited while at the destination
questions.memo: Secondary attractions are the extra places visited once the tourist is already there for the main (primary) reason.

questions.question: True or false: A museum is a natural attraction.
questions.memo: A museum is built by people, so it is a man-made attraction.

questions.question: True or false: The Drakensberg mountains are a natural attraction.
questions.memo: Mountains form in nature, so the Drakensberg is a natural attraction.

questions.question: An attraction built or created by people is called a _________ attraction.
questions.memo: Man-made attractions are constructed by people, such as theme parks, museums and monuments.

questions.question: A casino belongs to which attraction subsector?
questions.memo: Casinos fall under the gaming and lotteries subsector.

questions.question: A large conference centre belongs to which attraction subsector?
questions.memo: Conference and exhibition venues fall under the events and conferences subsector.

questions.question: Sort each attraction as man-made or natural.
questions.memo: Man-made attractions are built by people; natural attractions are formed by nature.

questions.question: A tourist travels to Cape Town mainly to attend a music festival, and while there also visits the V&A Waterfront. Sort these two attractions.

items.text: The music festival (the reason for the trip)

questions.memo: The primary attraction is the main reason for the trip (the festival); the secondary attraction is the extra visit made while there.

questions.question: Which activity is offered at a natural attraction like the Drakensberg?
options: Indoor ice skating in a mall
questions.memo: A natural attraction offers nature-based activities. At the Drakensberg, tourists can hike and watch birds.

questions.question: A nature reserve that protects wildlife belongs to which subsector?
questions.memo: Protecting wildlife and natural areas falls under the conservation subsector.

questions.question: A casino with gambling and entertainment would most appeal to which tourist?
options: A leisure or gaming tourist looking for entertainment
A tourist who only wants quiet nature walks
A tourist visiting solely for a business meeting
A tourist seeking a religious pilgrimage
questions.expected: A leisure or gaming tourist looking for entertainment
questions.memo: Linking an attraction to its appeal: a casino draws leisure and gaming tourists who want entertainment.

questions.question: During the 2010 FIFA World Cup, the matches were the _________ attraction, while game-park visits were secondary.
questions.memo: The World Cup was the main reason tourists came (primary); the game parks they also visited were secondary attractions.

questions.question: True or false: A single attraction can offer several different activities to tourists.
questions.memo: One attraction often offers many activities — for example a national park may offer game drives, hiking and bird-watching.

questions.question: Which is an example of the LEISURE subsector?
questions.memo: Leisure attractions, such as water parks and theme parks, exist mainly for fun and relaxation.

questions.question: A tourist travels to Durban for a wedding and also visits uShaka Marine World while there. uShaka Marine World is the:
questions.memo: The wedding is the primary reason for the trip; uShaka Marine World, visited while there, is the secondary attraction.

questions.question: Match each attraction to the tourist it would most appeal to.

items.text: A wildlife reserve focused on conservation

questions.memo: Link the attraction's appeal to the tourist type: thrills draw adventure tourists; heritage draws cultural tourists; protected nature draws eco-tourists.

questions.question: Why is it useful to classify attractions as primary or secondary?
options: It helps understand why tourists travel and how to plan and market trips
It sets the legal price of every ticket
It decides which attractions are allowed to open
questions.expected: It helps understand why tourists travel and how to plan and market trips
questions.memo: Knowing the main draw (primary) and the extras (secondary) helps the industry plan itineraries and market destinations effectively.

TOUR.G10.T1.INDUSTRY.A1.title: Structure of the SA tourism industry
TOUR.G10.T1.INDUSTRY.A1.description: Tourism as a partnership between the public sector (national/provincial/local government and parastatals), the private sector (product owners that profit from tourism) and local communities; the logo, function and service of key associations (TBCSA, TGCSA, FTTSA, SATSA, FEDHASA, ASATA).
TOUR.G10.T1.INDUSTRY.A1.recovery_strategy: Public sector = government and its agencies (funded by the state). Private sector = businesses that make a profit from tourism. Communities = the people living where tourism happens.

questions.question: Tourism in South Africa is a partnership between which three groups?
options: The public sector, the private sector and local communities
questions.expected: The public sector, the private sector and local communities
questions.memo: Tourism works as a partnership between government (public sector), profit-making businesses (private sector) and the communities where tourism happens.

questions.question: Which of these belongs to the PUBLIC sector?
questions.memo: Government departments such as the NDT are part of the public sector.

questions.question: Which of these belongs to the PRIVATE sector?
options: A privately owned tour operator that makes a profit
questions.expected: A privately owned tour operator that makes a profit
questions.memo: The private sector is made up of businesses that aim to make a profit from tourism, such as tour operators and travel agents.

questions.question: True or false: SANParks is a public entity (a government agency).
questions.memo: SANParks (South African National Parks) is a public entity that manages national parks on behalf of the state.

questions.question: What does ACSA stand for?
options: Association of Caterers in South Africa
questions.memo: ACSA (Airports Company South Africa) is a public entity that runs the country's major airports.

questions.question: What does TBCSA stand for?
options: Tourism Business Council of South Africa
Travel Bureau Centre of South Africa
Tourism Branding Committee of South Africa
Tour Bus Company of South Africa
questions.expected: Tourism Business Council of South Africa
questions.memo: The TBCSA is the umbrella body representing private-sector tourism businesses in South Africa.

questions.question: FEDHASA represents which part of the industry?
questions.memo: FEDHASA = Federated Hospitality Association of South Africa, representing the hospitality industry.

questions.question: ASATA represents which group?
options: Travel agents (Association of Southern African Travel Agents)
questions.expected: Travel agents (Association of Southern African Travel Agents)
questions.memo: ASATA = Association of Southern African Travel Agents, representing travel agents.

questions.question: What does FTTSA stand for?
options: Fair Trade in Tourism South Africa
Federation of Travel and Tourism South Africa
Foreign Tourism Trade of South Africa
Fast Track Travel of South Africa
questions.expected: Fair Trade in Tourism South Africa
questions.memo: FTTSA = Fair Trade in Tourism South Africa, which promotes fair and responsible tourism practices.

questions.question: Sort each organisation into the correct sector.

items.text: A guest house run for profit

questions.memo: Public sector = government and its agencies; private sector = businesses run for profit.

questions.question: True or false: A souvenir shop that makes a profit from tourists is part of the private sector.
questions.memo: Any business that profits from tourism — including a souvenir shop — is part of the private sector.

questions.question: Which government department handles passport applications for travellers?
questions.memo: Home Affairs issues passports and IDs, which travellers need for international travel.

questions.question: Which department assists South Africans with visa matters and emergencies abroad through embassies and consulates?
questions.memo: DIRCO runs South Africa's embassies and consulates, helping citizens with visas and emergencies overseas.

questions.question: A state-owned enterprise such as South African Airways is also called a _________.
questions.memo: A parastatal (state-owned enterprise) is a business owned by the government, such as South African Airways.

questions.question: How do local communities share in the benefits of tourism?
options: Through job creation, development, and better roads and schools
They receive no benefit at all
questions.expected: Through job creation, development, and better roads and schools
questions.memo: Communities benefit from tourism through jobs, local development and improved infrastructure such as roads and schools.

questions.question: Which body is responsible for grading accommodation establishments?
options: TGCSA (Tourism Grading Council of South Africa)
questions.expected: TGCSA (Tourism Grading Council of South Africa)
questions.memo: The TGCSA awards star grading to accommodation and venues.

questions.question: Match each association to the part of the industry it represents.
questions.memo: FEDHASA = hospitality; ASATA = travel agents; TGCSA = grading.

questions.question: True or false: The private sector in tourism aims to make a profit.
questions.memo: Private-sector tourism businesses exist to make a profit, unlike government bodies that provide services.

questions.question: Which is a benefit that tourism can bring to a local community?
options: New jobs and improved local services
questions.expected: New jobs and improved local services
questions.memo: Tourism can create jobs and bring money that improves services and infrastructure in a community.

questions.question: Which of these is an INTERNATIONAL tourism body?
questions.memo: The UNWTO is an international body; the others are South African organisations. International bodies include the UNWTO, WTTC and SADC.

TOUR.G10.T1.PAYMENT.A1.title: Payment methods & technology in South Africa
TOUR.G10.T1.PAYMENT.A1.description: Payment methods and the technology behind them (internet payments, ATMs, cellphone payments, fixed and portable speed points, credit cards, debit cards, cheques); their advantages and disadvantages; choosing the most appropriate method for a situation.
TOUR.G10.T1.PAYMENT.A1.recovery_strategy: A debit card spends YOUR OWN money already in the account; a credit card borrows the bank's money to be repaid later.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a debit card and a credit card?
options: A debit card spends your own money; a credit card borrows the bank's money to repay later
A debit card borrows money; a credit card spends your own money
A debit card can only be used overseas
questions.expected: A debit card spends your own money; a credit card borrows the bank's money to repay later
questions.memo: Debit = your own money already in the account. Credit = the bank's money, borrowed now and repaid later.

questions.question: What is a speed point machine?
options: A device that lets a business accept card payments
A machine that prints flight tickets
An ATM that gives out cash only
questions.expected: A device that lets a business accept card payments
questions.memo: A speed point (point-of-sale machine) reads credit and debit cards so a business can take card payments.

questions.question: True or false: A portable speed point can be brought to the customer, for example to a restaurant table.
questions.memo: Portable speed points are wireless, so staff can bring them to the table; fixed ones stay at the till.

questions.question: What is an advantage of paying by card instead of cash?
options: You do not have to carry large amounts of cash, which is safer
It always costs the business nothing
It works even with no electricity or signal
It cannot be traced if stolen
questions.expected: You do not have to carry large amounts of cash, which is safer
questions.memo: Card payments mean tourists carry less cash, lowering the risk of theft or loss.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of paying by cheque today?
options: Cheques are slow to clear and are no longer widely accepted
Cheques are the fastest payment method
questions.expected: Cheques are slow to clear and are no longer widely accepted
questions.memo: Cheques take days to clear and many businesses no longer accept them, making them an impractical choice.

questions.question: A _________ card spends money you already have in your bank account.
questions.memo: A debit card draws on money already in your own account.

questions.question: A _________ card lets you borrow the bank's money to pay now and repay later.
questions.memo: A credit card borrows from the bank, to be repaid later (sometimes with interest).

questions.question: Which of these is a credit card brand?
questions.memo: Credit card brands include Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Diners Club.

questions.question: What does a tourist typically do at an ATM?
questions.memo: An ATM (automated teller machine) lets people withdraw cash and do basic banking without a teller.

questions.question: Sort each payment method as mostly ELECTRONIC or CASH-BASED.

items.text: Tapping a card on a speed point
Withdrawing money to pay a street vendor

questions.memo: Electronic payments move money digitally (internet, card, cellphone); cash-based payments use physical notes and coins.

questions.question: What is a cellphone (mobile) payment?
options: Paying for goods or services using an app or service on your phone
Charging your phone at a hotel
questions.expected: Paying for goods or services using an app or service on your phone
questions.memo: Cellphone payments let tourists pay electronically through their mobile phone.

questions.question: True or false: Internet payments let a tourist pay for a booking online without using cash.
questions.memo: Internet payments are made online (for example when booking a hotel on a website), with no cash needed.

questions.question: A tourist wants to book and pay for a hotel from home before travelling. Which method is most appropriate?
options: An internet payment with a credit card
questions.expected: An internet payment with a credit card
questions.memo: Booking remotely suits an online payment by card — quick, secure and possible from anywhere.

questions.question: A tourist buys a snack from a small street vendor who has no card machine. Which payment is most appropriate?
options: A bank transfer that takes three days
questions.memo: A small vendor with no card machine is best paid in cash, which is immediate and needs no equipment.

questions.question: Match each situation to the most appropriate payment method.

items.text: Buying fruit from a roadside stall
Paying a restaurant bill at the table
Booking a flight on a website
Tipping a small amount to a porter
Reserving a hotel room online in advance

questions.memo: Match the method to the setting: cash for small in-person amounts; card for in-store/at-table; internet for remote online bookings.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of carrying large amounts of cash while travelling?
options: It can be lost or stolen, with little chance of getting it back
It cannot be spent on small items
questions.expected: It can be lost or stolen, with little chance of getting it back
questions.memo: Cash is risky to carry in large amounts because, if lost or stolen, it usually cannot be recovered.

questions.question: True or false: A debit card normally lets you spend more money than you have in your account.
questions.memo: A debit card can normally only spend money you actually have. Borrowing beyond your balance is what a credit card allows.

questions.question: The SA Travel Card is an example of a _________ card.
questions.memo: The SA Travel Card is a prepaid debit card — you load your own money onto it before spending.

questions.question: What is an advantage of a portable speed point for a tourism business?
options: Staff can take card payments anywhere, such as at the table or on a tour
It removes the need for any electricity or network
It guarantees the business pays no fees
questions.expected: Staff can take card payments anywhere, such as at the table or on a tour
questions.memo: A portable speed point lets a business accept card payments away from the till, improving convenience for customers.

questions.question: Sort each statement as an ADVANTAGE or DISADVANTAGE of card payments.

items.text: No need to carry large amounts of cash
Will not work if the network or power is down
Payments are quick and can be traced if needed
The business may pay transaction fees

questions.memo: Cards are safer and quicker than cash (advantages) but depend on power and a network and may carry fees (disadvantages).

TOUR.G10.T2.MAPTERMS.A1.title: Map terminology & symbols
TOUR.G10.T2.MAPTERMS.A1.description: Map concepts: scale, direction, distance indicators, legends, grid references, equator, hemispheres, poles, latitude, longitude, time zones, Universal Time Coordinate (UTC) and the International Date Line (IDL).
TOUR.G10.T2.MAPTERMS.A1.recovery_strategy: Latitude lines run across (like rungs of a ladder, measuring north-south position); longitude lines run top-to-bottom between the poles (measuring east-west position).

questions.question: What does the SCALE of a map tell you?
options: How distance on the map relates to real distance on the ground
questions.expected: How distance on the map relates to real distance on the ground
questions.memo: Scale links map distance to real distance — for example 1 cm on the map might represent 10 km on the ground.

questions.question: What is the LEGEND (key) of a map?
options: A box that explains what the symbols on the map mean
questions.expected: A box that explains what the symbols on the map mean
questions.memo: The legend or key explains the symbols and colours used on the map.

questions.question: What is the equator?
options: An imaginary line that divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres
The line where the date changes
questions.expected: An imaginary line that divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres
questions.memo: The equator (0° latitude) circles the Earth halfway between the poles, splitting it into northern and southern hemispheres.

questions.question: Lines that run east-west and measure how far north or south a place is are called lines of _________.
questions.memo: Lines of latitude run east-west (like rungs of a ladder) and measure position north or south of the equator.

questions.question: Lines that run between the North and South Poles and measure east-west position are called lines of _________.
questions.memo: Lines of longitude run from pole to pole and measure position east or west of the Prime Meridian.

questions.question: True or false: Lines of longitude run east to west.
questions.memo: Lines of longitude run north-south (pole to pole). Lines of latitude run east-west.

questions.question: What is a 'hemisphere'?
options: One half of the Earth (such as the northern or southern half)
questions.expected: One half of the Earth (such as the northern or southern half)
questions.memo: A hemisphere is half of the globe — the equator divides north from south, and the Prime Meridian helps divide east from west.

questions.question: What is a grid reference used for on a map?
options: To locate a point using lettered and numbered lines
To show the price of the map
questions.expected: To locate a point using lettered and numbered lines
questions.memo: A grid divides the map into squares; a grid reference (such as B4) pinpoints where to find a place.

questions.question: What is the International Date Line (IDL)?
options: An imaginary line where the calendar date changes by one day
questions.expected: An imaginary line where the calendar date changes by one day
questions.memo: The IDL runs roughly down the middle of the Pacific Ocean; crossing it changes the date by a day.

questions.question: What does UTC stand for?
questions.memo: UTC (Universal Time Coordinated) is the world time standard against which time zones are measured.

questions.question: True or false: The equator lies at 0° latitude.
questions.memo: The equator is the line of 0° latitude, halfway between the poles.

questions.question: The most northern point of the Earth is the _________ Pole.
questions.memo: The North Pole is the northernmost point; the South Pole is the southernmost.

questions.question: A compass rose on a map shows:
questions.memo: A compass rose indicates direction so you can orient the map.

questions.question: Sort each term as a LOCATION concept or a TIME concept.
questions.memo: Latitude, longitude and grid references locate places; time zones, the IDL and UTC deal with time.

questions.question: What does a distance indicator (scale bar) on a map let you do?
options: Work out the real distance between two places on the map
Find the name of the cartographer
questions.expected: Work out the real distance between two places on the map
questions.memo: A distance indicator or scale bar lets you measure map distance and convert it to real distance.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa lies in the Southern Hemisphere.
questions.memo: South Africa is south of the equator, so it is in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.question: The line of 0° longitude is called the _________ Meridian.
questions.memo: The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) passes through Greenwich and is the starting point for measuring longitude.

questions.question: Why are symbols useful on a map?
options: They show real features (airports, roads, rivers) in a simple, compact way
They make the map more expensive
They hide information from the reader
They replace the need for a title
questions.expected: They show real features (airports, roads, rivers) in a simple, compact way
questions.memo: Symbols let a map represent many features clearly without writing out long descriptions.

questions.question: Match each map term to its meaning.

items.text: Relates map distance to real distance
Locates a point using rows and columns
Tells you 1 cm equals a number of kilometres
A key to the colours and symbols

questions.memo: Scale = map-to-real distance; legend = symbol key; grid reference = a position from rows and columns.

questions.question: Another name for a map's legend is the:
questions.memo: The legend is also called the key — both explain the map's symbols.

TOUR.G10.T2.MAPTYPES.A1.title: Types of maps in a tourism context
TOUR.G10.T2.MAPTYPES.A1.description: Road/street maps, political maps, physical maps, specialist maps (climate, airports, railways), tourist information maps, and electronic maps (GPS, Google Maps, Google Earth) — their uses and value in tourism.
TOUR.G10.T2.MAPTYPES.A1.recovery_strategy: Match the map to the question: borders/capitals = political; landforms = physical; getting from A to B = road/GPS; attractions in an area = tourist information map.

questions.question: What does a POLITICAL map mainly show?
options: Countries, borders, provinces and capital cities
Mountains, rivers and the height of land
questions.expected: Countries, borders, provinces and capital cities
questions.memo: Political maps show human-made divisions: countries, provinces, borders and capitals.

questions.question: What does a PHYSICAL map mainly show?
options: Natural features such as mountains, rivers and the height of land
Country borders and capital cities only
questions.expected: Natural features such as mountains, rivers and the height of land
questions.memo: Physical maps show natural landforms — mountains, rivers, valleys and elevation.

questions.question: A road or street map is most useful for:
options: Planning a driving route from one place to another
questions.expected: Planning a driving route from one place to another
questions.memo: Road and street maps show roads and routes, which is what you need to plan a drive.

questions.question: A tourist information map typically shows:
options: Attractions, parks, trails and points of interest in an area
questions.expected: Attractions, parks, trails and points of interest in an area
questions.memo: Tourist information maps highlight what visitors want — attractions, national parks, trails and sights.

questions.question: What does a GPS (global positioning system) do for a traveller?
options: Shows their location and gives directions using satellites
questions.expected: Shows their location and gives directions using satellites
questions.memo: A GPS uses satellites to pinpoint your location and guide you with turn-by-turn directions.

questions.question: True or false: Google Earth is an example of an electronic map resource.
questions.memo: Google Earth, Google Maps and GPS are all electronic (digital) map resources.

questions.question: Which of these is a SPECIALIST map?
options: A climate map showing rainfall and temperature
A street map of a town
questions.expected: A climate map showing rainfall and temperature
questions.memo: Specialist maps focus on one theme, such as climate, airports or railways.

questions.question: A map that shows mountains, rivers and the height of the land is a _________ map.
questions.memo: Physical maps show natural landforms and elevation.

questions.question: Which map would you use to find a country's capital city?
questions.memo: Capitals and borders are shown on political maps.

questions.question: Which map would you use to plan a driving route between two cities?
questions.memo: Road maps (or GPS) show the roads needed to plan a drive.

questions.question: Match each task to the most suitable map.

items.text: Find which province a city is in
See where the mountain ranges are
Find the attractions near a town
Locate the nearest national park and trail

questions.memo: Borders and capitals = political; landforms = physical; attractions and trails = tourist information.

questions.question: True or false: A GPS can give turn-by-turn directions while you travel.
questions.memo: A GPS guides you step by step, telling you when to turn as you drive.

questions.question: What is an advantage of electronic maps over paper maps?
options: They can update in real time and give live directions and traffic
They never need a device or battery
They cannot be zoomed in or out
They always work without any signal
questions.expected: They can update in real time and give live directions and traffic
questions.memo: Electronic maps update live, show traffic and guide you — advantages a paper map cannot offer.

questions.question: A map showing tourist attractions, hiking trails and national parks is a tourist _________ map.
questions.memo: Tourist information maps point out attractions, trails and parks for visitors.

questions.question: Which map shows climate features such as rainfall and temperature?
questions.memo: A climate map is a specialist map focused on weather-related information.

questions.question: True or false: A political map is the best choice for finding the height of mountains.
questions.memo: Heights of mountains are shown on a physical map, not a political one.

questions.question: What is the main VALUE of maps in tourism?
options: They help tourists find their way, plan routes and locate attractions
They replace the need for any transport
They set the prices of hotels
questions.expected: They help tourists find their way, plan routes and locate attractions
questions.memo: Maps help with orientation, route planning and finding what to see — essential tools for travel.

questions.question: Sort each map resource as PAPER or ELECTRONIC.
questions.memo: Paper maps are printed; electronic maps are digital tools such as GPS, Google Maps and Google Earth.

questions.question: A smartphone app that guides a tourist to a restaurant relies on _________.
questions.memo: Navigation apps use GPS (satellite positioning) to locate the user and give directions.

questions.question: Which map would best help a visitor find national parks and attractions in a province?
questions.memo: Tourist information maps are designed to show attractions and parks for visitors.

TOUR.G10.T2.SAMAP.A1.title: Locating features on a map of South Africa
TOUR.G10.T2.SAMAP.A1.description: Locating South Africa's borders, provinces, capital cities, international airports, harbours, national highways, gateways, major mountains, rivers and dams on a colour map.
TOUR.G10.T2.SAMAP.A1.recovery_strategy: Build a mental map from the coast inward: coastal provinces (WC, EC, KZN) ring the south and east; the interior holds Free State, Gauteng, North West, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and Northern Cape.

questions.question: Which of these is a COASTAL province of South Africa?
questions.memo: KwaZulu-Natal lies on the east coast. Gauteng, Free State and Mpumalanga are inland.

questions.question: In which city is Table Mountain found?
questions.memo: Table Mountain overlooks Cape Town in the Western Cape.

questions.question: Which of these provinces is land-locked (has no coastline)?
questions.memo: Gauteng is inland with no coast. Western Cape, Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal all border the sea.

questions.question: OR Tambo International Airport is located in which province?
questions.memo: OR Tambo, the country's busiest airport, is in Gauteng (near Johannesburg).

questions.question: Which city has one of South Africa's busiest harbours on the east coast?
questions.memo: Durban has one of the largest and busiest ports in Africa, on the east coast.

questions.question: True or false: Gauteng is a coastal province.
questions.memo: Gauteng is inland and has no coastline.

questions.question: South Africa's largest and busiest port city on the east coast is _________.
questions.memo: Durban's harbour is the busiest on the east coast.

questions.question: Which group lists THREE of South Africa's coastal provinces?
questions.memo: The coastal provinces are Western Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and the Northern Cape (west coast).

questions.question: Sort each province as COASTAL or INLAND.
questions.memo: Coastal provinces touch the sea (Western Cape, Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Northern Cape); the rest are inland.

questions.question: Which group correctly names South Africa's three capital cities?
questions.memo: South Africa has three capitals: Pretoria (executive), Cape Town (legislative) and Bloemfontein (judicial).

questions.question: True or false: Pretoria is the executive (administrative) capital of South Africa.
questions.memo: Pretoria is the executive capital, home to the government's administration.

questions.question: The V&A Waterfront and Robben Island are attractions in which city?
questions.memo: Both the V&A Waterfront and Robben Island are in Cape Town.

questions.question: The executive (administrative) capital of South Africa is _________.
questions.memo: Pretoria is the executive capital.

questions.question: Which of these is a major river in South Africa?
questions.memo: The Orange River is South Africa's longest river. The others are in other parts of the world.

questions.question: King Shaka International Airport serves which city?
questions.memo: King Shaka International Airport serves Durban in KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: Match each landmark or airport to its province.
questions.memo: Anchor each feature to its city and province: Cape Town = Western Cape; Johannesburg = Gauteng; Durban = KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: True or false: The Northern Cape is the largest South African province by area.
questions.memo: The Northern Cape is the largest province by land area, though it has a small population.

questions.question: Which country lies directly to the north of South Africa and is a popular tourism gateway by road?
