questions.memo: Zimbabwe borders South Africa to the north (across the Limpopo River). Botswana also borders the north-west.

questions.question: Cape Town International Airport is located in which province?
questions.memo: Cape Town International Airport is in the Western Cape.

questions.question: Match each province to its capital city.
questions.memo: Western Cape = Cape Town; KwaZulu-Natal = Pietermaritzburg; Free State = Bloemfontein.

TOUR.G10.T2.WORLDMAP.A1.title: Locating SADC, continents, oceans & tourism regions
TOUR.G10.T2.WORLDMAP.A1.description: Locating South Africa and the SADC countries, the seven continents, three oceans, island groups and the major tourism regions (Far East, Middle East, UK, Europe, the Americas, Australasia) on a colour map of the world.
TOUR.G10.T2.WORLDMAP.A1.recovery_strategy: There are 7 continents (fixed) and 3 oceans; tourism regions are travel-industry groupings of countries within or across continents.

questions.question: How many continents are there on Earth?
questions.memo: The seven continents are Asia, Africa, Europe, North America, South America, Australia and Antarctica.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a continent?
questions.memo: Western Europe is a tourism region within the continent of Europe, not a continent itself.

questions.question: Which three oceans does the CAPS curriculum focus on?
questions.memo: The three main oceans studied are the Indian, Atlantic and Pacific.

questions.question: Which ocean lies along South Africa's EAST coast?
questions.memo: The Indian Ocean washes South Africa's east coast (Durban side); the Atlantic is on the west (Cape Town side).

questions.question: Which of these is a SADC country bordering South Africa?
questions.memo: Botswana is a SADC member that borders South Africa. Kenya, Egypt and Nigeria are elsewhere in Africa.

questions.question: True or false: Australia is both a country and a continent.
questions.memo: Australia is the only place that is both a single country and a continent.

questions.question: The ocean along South Africa's WEST coast is the _________ Ocean.
questions.memo: The Atlantic Ocean lies on South Africa's west coast.

questions.question: Sort each country as a SADC member or NOT a SADC member.
questions.memo: SADC is the Southern African Development Community — neighbours like Namibia, Zimbabwe, Botswana and Mozambique. France and Japan are far outside the region.

questions.question: Which of these is a tourism REGION (not a continent)?
questions.memo: The Far East is a travel-industry region; the others are continents.

questions.question: South Africa is located on which continent?
questions.memo: South Africa is at the southern tip of the continent of Africa.

questions.question: True or false: Brazil is a country in South America.
questions.memo: Brazil is the largest country in South America.

questions.question: The United Kingdom lies in which part of the world?
questions.memo: The United Kingdom is in Europe and is treated as its own tourism region.

questions.question: Match each country to its continent.
questions.memo: Place each country on its continent: South Africa and Kenya in Africa; Brazil and Argentina in South America; China in Asia.

questions.question: The largest continent by area is _________.
questions.memo: Asia is the largest continent in both area and population.

questions.question: Australia and New Zealand belong to which tourism region?
questions.memo: Australasia covers Australia, New Zealand and neighbouring Pacific islands.

questions.question: True or false: A tourism region and a continent are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: A tourism region is a travel-industry grouping of countries (like Western Europe), which can be smaller than, or cross, continents.

questions.question: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
questions.memo: The Indian Ocean sits between the east of Africa and Australia.

questions.question: Sort each item as a CONTINENT, an OCEAN or a TOURISM REGION.
questions.memo: Continents and oceans are fixed geographic features; tourism regions (like the Middle East or Western Europe) are industry groupings.

questions.question: Which list contains only SADC neighbours of South Africa?
questions.memo: Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Mozambique all border South Africa and are SADC members.

questions.question: Antarctica is best described as:
questions.memo: Antarctica is the icy continent at the far south of the globe.

TOUR.G10.T2.DISTANCE.A1.title: Distance indicators & distance tables
TOUR.G10.T2.DISTANCE.A1.description: Using distance indicators on maps and distance tables to work out distances between towns and cities, and linking distance to travelling time (roughly 100 km per hour).
TOUR.G10.T2.DISTANCE.A1.recovery_strategy: Find one city on the top and the other down the side; the cell where the row and column meet is the distance. Divide km by 100 for an approximate drive in hours.

questions.question: At an average of about 100 km per hour, roughly how long does a 300 km drive take?
questions.memo: Divide distance by 100: 300 ÷ 100 = about 3 hours.

questions.question: What does a distance indicator on a map show?
questions.memo: A distance indicator helps you work out how far apart two places are.

questions.question: True or false: As a rough guide, you can drive about 100 km in one hour.
questions.memo: The CAPS rule of thumb is roughly 100 km per hour, useful for estimating travel time.

questions.question: To read a distance table, you find one city along the top and the other down the side, then read the cell where the row and _________ meet.
questions.memo: The distance is in the cell where the chosen row and column cross.

questions.question: Johannesburg to Durban is about 570 km. Roughly how long is the drive?
questions.memo: 570 ÷ 100 ≈ 5.7, so about 5 to 6 hours of driving.

questions.question: On a distance table, the number printed where two cities meet represents:
options: The distance in kilometres between those two cities
The cost of a bus ticket
questions.expected: The distance in kilometres between those two cities
questions.memo: Distance tables show the kilometres between pairs of cities.

questions.question: At about 100 km/h, roughly how long is a 200 km trip?
questions.memo: 200 ÷ 100 = about 2 hours.

questions.question: True or false: A distance table gives the distance in kilometres between major cities.
questions.memo: Distance tables list the kilometres between pairs of major towns and cities.

questions.question: At about 100 km/h, a 400 km journey takes roughly _________ hours.
questions.memo: 400 ÷ 100 = about 4 hours.

questions.question: Match each distance to its approximate driving time (at about 100 km/h).
questions.memo: Divide each distance by 100 to estimate the hours of driving.

questions.question: Why is working out distance and travel time important when planning a tour?
options: So each day's travel is realistic and not too rushed
So the tour can ignore where attractions are
So tourists never need to sleep
So the bus can skip all stops
questions.expected: So each day's travel is realistic and not too rushed
questions.memo: Knowing how far and how long lets a planner build a comfortable, realistic daily schedule.

questions.question: At about 100 km/h, roughly how long is a 150 km trip?
questions.memo: 150 ÷ 100 = 1.5, so about one and a half hours.

questions.question: True or false: If all else is equal, a longer distance means a longer travelling time.
questions.memo: At a steady speed, more kilometres take more time.

questions.question: At about 100 km/h, which is the best estimate of the time for a 250 km trip?
questions.memo: 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5, so about two and a half hours.

questions.question: At about 100 km/h, a 600 km journey takes roughly _________ hours.
questions.memo: 600 ÷ 100 = about 6 hours.

questions.question: A scale bar (distance indicator) on a map lets you:
options: Measure the real distance between two places on the map
Find the names of the streets
questions.expected: Measure the real distance between two places on the map
questions.memo: A scale bar converts the gap on the map into a real-world distance.

questions.question: Sort each trip as a likely DAY TRIP or one that NEEDS AN OVERNIGHT STAY (at about 100 km/h, one-way).
questions.memo: Short distances (under ~150 km) suit a day trip; very long ones (many hours each way) need an overnight stay.

questions.question: When planning a tour route, why should you allow time for stops?
options: For rest, meals and comfort breaks so the trip is enjoyable
To make the trip as tiring as possible
Because stops are not allowed on tours
To avoid reaching the destination at all
questions.expected: For rest, meals and comfort breaks so the trip is enjoyable
questions.memo: Real journeys include rest, fuel and meal stops, which add to the total time and keep travellers comfortable.

questions.question: True or false: To use a distance table you must find BOTH cities — one on the top and one on the side.
questions.memo: You locate both cities (row and column); their meeting cell gives the distance.

questions.question: If 100 km takes about 1 hour, roughly how long is a 350 km trip?
questions.memo: 350 ÷ 100 = 3.5, so about three and a half hours.

TOUR.G10.T2.DOMESTIC.A1.title: Domestic tourism — concepts, benefits & Sho't Left
TOUR.G10.T2.DOMESTIC.A1.description: The concept of domestic tourism; its benefits for South Africa's economy, people and environment; and the Sho't Left campaign that promotes travel within South Africa.
TOUR.G10.T2.DOMESTIC.A1.recovery_strategy: Domestic tourism = residents travelling WITHIN their own country. Sho't Left encourages South Africans to take affordable local trips.

questions.question: What is domestic tourism?
options: Residents travelling within their own country
questions.expected: Residents travelling within their own country
questions.memo: Domestic tourism is people travelling within their own country — for example South Africans holidaying in South Africa.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the Sho't Left campaign?
options: To encourage South Africans to travel within South Africa
questions.expected: To encourage South Africans to travel within South Africa
questions.memo: Sho't Left encourages South Africans to take affordable trips within their own country.

questions.question: What is a benefit of domestic tourism for South Africa's ECONOMY?
options: Tourists' spending stays in the country and supports local jobs
questions.expected: Tourists' spending stays in the country and supports local jobs
questions.memo: When residents holiday at home, their spending stays in the local economy, supporting businesses and jobs.

questions.question: True or false: Domestic tourism only benefits foreign countries.
questions.memo: Domestic tourism benefits the home country — its economy, people and communities.

questions.question: Sho't Left encourages South Africans to take affordable _________ trips.
questions.memo: The campaign promotes affordable local travel within South Africa.

questions.question: How does domestic tourism benefit PEOPLE and communities?
options: It creates jobs and builds skills in local communities
It only helps large foreign companies
It has no effect on people
questions.expected: It creates jobs and builds skills in local communities
questions.memo: Domestic tourism creates employment and develops skills for people in the places tourists visit.

questions.question: Which is a way responsible domestic tourism can benefit the ENVIRONMENT?
options: Income from visitors helps fund the upkeep of parks and nature reserves
It uses no resources at all
questions.expected: Income from visitors helps fund the upkeep of parks and nature reserves
questions.memo: Money from tourists visiting parks and reserves can help pay for conservation and upkeep.

questions.question: True or false: Domestic tourism means travelling within your own country.
questions.memo: Domestic = within the home country.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Domestic tourism is good for South Africa's economy.

pool.text: Local spending stays in the country and circulates in the economy
It creates and protects jobs in transport, accommodation and attractions
It keeps the industry going even when foreign arrivals drop
Some South Africans enjoy taking photographs
Aeroplanes are painted in different colours

questions.memo: The strong points all link domestic tourism to money and jobs staying in the country. The red herrings are true statements that do not support the economic argument.

questions.question: Which organisation runs the Sho't Left campaign?
questions.memo: SA Tourism runs the Sho't Left campaign to promote domestic travel.

questions.question: Sort each benefit of domestic tourism under the area it mainly helps.

items.text: Spending circulates in the local economy
Jobs and skills for local residents
Builds pride in local culture and heritage

questions.memo: Group benefits by the three areas CAPS lists: economy, people and the environment.

questions.question: Which is an example of a domestic tourist?
options: A Johannesburg family on holiday in the Western Cape
A German couple visiting Cape Town
A South African studying in Australia
A tourist from Brazil at Kruger Park
questions.expected: A Johannesburg family on holiday in the Western Cape
questions.memo: A domestic tourist travels within their own country — here, South Africans travelling inside South Africa.

questions.question: When South Africans holiday at home, their money stays in the local _________.
questions.memo: Domestic spending keeps money circulating in the local economy.

questions.question: True or false: Encouraging off-peak travel can help reduce the problem of seasonality in domestic tourism.
questions.memo: If people travel in quieter seasons too, business is spread more evenly through the year, easing seasonality.

questions.question: Why does the government promote domestic tourism?
options: To spread tourism's benefits and support the economy and jobs
To send money out of the country
questions.expected: To spread tourism's benefits and support the economy and jobs
questions.memo: Promoting local travel spreads income and jobs across the country and strengthens the tourism economy.

questions.question: Why is domestic tourism especially valuable when international travel drops (for example during a global crisis)?
options: Local travellers keep the tourism industry running and protect jobs
It makes no difference at all
It forces businesses to close faster
questions.expected: Local travellers keep the tourism industry running and protect jobs
questions.memo: When foreign arrivals fall, domestic tourists help keep accommodation, attractions and transport in business.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about domestic tourism.

items.text: It is travel within your own country
It keeps spending in the local economy

questions.memo: Domestic tourism is home-country travel that benefits the local economy and is promoted by Sho't Left.

questions.question: The name 'Sho't Left' comes from South African slang meaning to:
options: Take a short, nearby trip (originally asking a taxi to stop just ahead)
questions.expected: Take a short, nearby trip (originally asking a taxi to stop just ahead)
questions.memo: 'Sho't left' is taxi slang for stopping just ahead — the campaign uses it to mean taking an easy, affordable local trip.

questions.question: Which is the STRONGEST reason that domestic tourism matters to South Africa?
options: It keeps money and jobs inside the country and supports the whole industry
It gives people something to photograph
questions.expected: It keeps money and jobs inside the country and supports the whole industry
questions.memo: The core value is economic: local spending sustains jobs and the tourism industry nationwide.

questions.question: Domestic tourism most directly supports:
questions.memo: Domestic tourists spend at local establishments, supporting community jobs and small businesses.

TOUR.G10.T2.DOMSTATS.A1.title: Interpreting domestic tourism statistics
TOUR.G10.T2.DOMSTATS.A1.description: Concepts of statistics and intra- vs inter-provincial travel; interpreting statistics on purpose of trips, most-visited provinces, length of stay, average expenditure and seasonality.
TOUR.G10.T2.DOMSTATS.A1.recovery_strategy: Intra- = WITHIN one province (intra = inside). Inter- = BETWEEN provinces. Read graph titles and axes before drawing a conclusion.

questions.question: What does 'intra-provincial' travel mean?
questions.memo: Intra- means 'within'. Intra-provincial travel stays inside one province.

questions.question: What does 'inter-provincial' travel mean?
questions.memo: Inter- means 'between'. Inter-provincial travel crosses from one province to another.

questions.question: True or false: A trip from Gauteng to KwaZulu-Natal is intra-provincial travel.
questions.memo: Gauteng to KwaZulu-Natal crosses provinces, so it is inter-provincial (between provinces).

questions.question: Travel WITHIN one province is called _________-provincial travel.
questions.memo: Intra-provincial = within one province.

questions.question: What do tourism statistics mainly help the industry and government to do?
options: Make informed decisions and plan for the future
Decide what colour to paint buses
Replace the need for any tourism
questions.expected: Make informed decisions and plan for the future
questions.memo: Statistics reveal patterns (who travels, where, how long, how much they spend) that guide planning and decisions.

questions.question: In tourism statistics, 'length of stay' means:
options: The number of nights a tourist stays
The number of tourists in a group
questions.expected: The number of nights a tourist stays
questions.memo: Length of stay measures how many nights tourists spend at a destination.

questions.question: What does 'seasonality' mean in tourism?
options: Tourism being busier at certain times of the year than others
The weather being the same all year
Tourists only travelling once in a lifetime
The number of seasons in a country
questions.expected: Tourism being busier at certain times of the year than others
questions.memo: Seasonality describes peaks and troughs — for example coastal towns being full in summer holidays and quiet in winter.

questions.question: True or false: 'Average expenditure per tourist' is the typical amount each tourist spends.
questions.memo: Average expenditure per tourist shows the typical spend of one tourist, useful for measuring economic value.

questions.question: A bar graph shows the Western Cape with the tallest bar for 'most-visited province'. This means the Western Cape:
options: Received the most domestic visitors of the provinces shown
questions.expected: Received the most domestic visitors of the provinces shown
questions.memo: On a bar graph, the tallest bar represents the largest value — here, the most visitors.

questions.question: Sort each example as INTRA-provincial or INTER-provincial travel.

items.text: Cape Town to Stellenbosch (both Western Cape)

questions.memo: Within one province = intra; across provinces = inter.

questions.question: A trip from Cape Town to Johannesburg is _________-provincial travel.
questions.memo: Cape Town (Western Cape) to Johannesburg (Gauteng) crosses provinces, so it is inter-provincial.

questions.question: Why does seasonality matter to a tourism business?
options: It helps the business plan staffing, stock and prices for busy and quiet times
It tells the business what colour to paint the walls
It has no effect on a business
questions.expected: It helps the business plan staffing, stock and prices for busy and quiet times
questions.memo: Knowing peak and off-peak periods lets a business plan staff, supplies and pricing.

questions.question: True or false: Statistics are numerical facts or data collected about something.
questions.memo: Statistics are collected numbers and data that can be analysed to find patterns.

questions.question: If a graph shows December as the busiest travel month at a coastal town, this is an example of:
questions.memo: A busy December at the coast reflects seasonality — the summer-holiday high season.

questions.question: Which statistic describes the reason tourists made their trips (for example leisure, VFR or business)?
questions.memo: 'Purpose of trip' statistics show why people travelled — for leisure, to visit family, for business and so on.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about reading tourism statistics.

items.text: On a bar graph, a taller bar means a larger value
You should read the title and axes before drawing a conclusion
The shortest bar always shows the most visitors
Statistics can reveal patterns and trends
Graph titles and labels can be ignored

questions.memo: Read graphs carefully — title, axes and labels first — and remember taller bars mean larger values.

questions.question: If a table shows that province A has a higher average expenditure per tourist than province B, this suggests:
options: Tourists typically spend more per person in province A
Province B is larger in area
questions.expected: Tourists typically spend more per person in province A
questions.memo: Higher average expenditure means each tourist tends to spend more in that province.

questions.question: True or false: Generally, the more nights tourists stay, the more money they tend to spend locally.
questions.memo: Longer stays usually mean more spending on accommodation, meals and activities, benefiting the local economy.

questions.question: The number of nights a tourist stays is called the length of _________.
questions.memo: Length of stay = number of nights spent at the destination.

questions.question: Why does the government collect tourism statistics?
options: To measure how the industry is doing and plan for its growth
questions.expected: To measure how the industry is doing and plan for its growth
questions.memo: Government uses statistics to track the industry's performance and to plan policies that help it grow.

TOUR.G10.T3.PROVATTR.A1.title: Tourist attractions in the provinces of South Africa
TOUR.G10.T3.PROVATTR.A1.description: Key attractions in each of the nine provinces — their location (nearest city/town) and main focus — including World Heritage Sites such as the Cradle of Humankind, Robben Island, iSimangaliso and Mapungubwe.
TOUR.G10.T3.PROVATTR.A1.recovery_strategy: Anchor each attraction to its nearest major city, then to that city's province (Table Mountain - Cape Town - Western Cape).

questions.question: In which province is Table Mountain located?
questions.memo: Table Mountain rises above Cape Town in the Western Cape.

questions.question: The Apartheid Museum and Gold Reef City are found in which province?
questions.memo: Both are in Johannesburg, Gauteng.

questions.question: The Big Hole and Mine Museum at Kimberley are in which province?
questions.memo: Kimberley, home of the Big Hole, is in the Northern Cape.

questions.question: Sun City and the Pilanesberg Game Reserve are located in which province?
questions.memo: Sun City and Pilanesberg are in the North West province.

questions.question: The Cango Caves and the Garden Route are attractions in which province?
questions.memo: The Cango Caves (near Oudtshoorn) and much of the Garden Route are in the Western Cape.

questions.question: uShaka Marine World and the Golden Mile beachfront are found in which province?
questions.memo: Both are in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: The Panorama Route, including the Blyde River Canyon and God's Window, is in which province?
questions.memo: The Panorama Route and Blyde River Canyon are in Mpumalanga.

questions.question: The Addo Elephant National Park is in which province?
questions.memo: Addo Elephant National Park is in the Eastern Cape, near Gqeberha.

questions.question: Golden Gate Highlands National Park is found in which province?
questions.memo: Golden Gate Highlands National Park, known for its sandstone cliffs, is in the Free State.

questions.question: True or false: Robben Island is an attraction in the Western Cape.
questions.memo: Robben Island lies in Table Bay off Cape Town, in the Western Cape.

questions.question: True or false: The Cradle of Humankind is located in KwaZulu-Natal.
questions.memo: The Cradle of Humankind is in Gauteng, not KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: The V&A Waterfront is located in the city of _________.
questions.memo: The V&A Waterfront is on Cape Town's harbour.

questions.question: The Comrades Marathon is run between Durban and Pietermaritzburg in the province of _________.
questions.memo: The Comrades Marathon takes place in KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: Match each attraction to its province.
questions.memo: Anchor each to its city: Cape Town = Western Cape; Johannesburg = Gauteng; Durban / Drakensberg = KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: Match each attraction to its province.
questions.memo: Addo and Bloukrans = Eastern Cape; Golden Gate = Free State; the Panorama Route (Blyde River Canyon, God's Window) = Mpumalanga.

questions.question: The spring wildflower displays of Namaqualand are a famous attraction in which province?
questions.memo: Namaqualand's spring flowers are mainly in the Northern Cape (extending into the Western Cape).

questions.question: The Mapungubwe Cultural Landscape is located in which province?
questions.memo: Mapungubwe, a World Heritage Site, is in Limpopo near the Botswana and Zimbabwe borders.

questions.question: Which of these South African attractions is a declared World Heritage Site?
questions.memo: The Cradle of Humankind is a World Heritage Site; the others are popular but not World Heritage Sites.

questions.question: The uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park is located in which province?
questions.memo: The uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park, a World Heritage Site, is in KwaZulu-Natal.

questions.question: A tourist wants to visit the Kruger National Park. Which provinces does it mainly fall within?
questions.memo: The Kruger National Park stretches across Limpopo and Mpumalanga in the north-east of the country.

TOUR.G10.T3.SANPARKS.A1.title: SANParks, transfrontier parks & private reserves
TOUR.G10.T3.SANPARKS.A1.description: What a national park is and why tourists visit; Kruger as the flagship; other national parks and their conservation focus; transfrontier parks and conservation areas; and luxury private game reserves (Shamwari, Madikwe, Phinda, Sabi Sabi).
TOUR.G10.T3.SANPARKS.A1.recovery_strategy: A transfrontier park crosses an international BORDER and is shared by two or more countries; a national park sits within one country.

questions.question: What is a national park?
options: A protected area conserved by the state for nature and wildlife
A shopping centre in a city
questions.expected: A protected area conserved by the state for nature and wildlife
questions.memo: A national park is land protected by the state to conserve nature, wildlife and habitats for the public to enjoy.

questions.question: Which national park is regarded as SANParks' flagship park?
questions.memo: The Kruger National Park is the flagship of South African National Parks (SANParks).

questions.question: Why do tourists visit national parks?
options: To see wildlife and enjoy nature in a protected setting
To watch films at a cinema
questions.expected: To see wildlife and enjoy nature in a protected setting
questions.memo: National parks attract tourists who want to experience wildlife and natural landscapes.

questions.question: In the Kruger National Park, which rest camp serves as the administrative headquarters and is the largest camp?
questions.memo: Skukuza is Kruger's largest rest camp and its administrative headquarters.

questions.question: What is a transfrontier park?
options: A conservation area that crosses the border between two or more countries
A park found only inside one city
questions.expected: A conservation area that crosses the border between two or more countries
questions.memo: A transfrontier park spans an international border and is shared and managed by more than one country.

questions.question: True or false: The Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park is shared between South Africa and Botswana.
questions.memo: The Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park is jointly managed by South Africa and Botswana.

questions.question: True or false: A transfrontier park lies entirely within South Africa.
questions.memo: By definition a transfrontier park crosses a border, so it spans more than one country.

questions.question: What is a luxury private game reserve?
options: A privately owned reserve offering exclusive, high-end wildlife experiences
A free public park with no facilities
questions.expected: A privately owned reserve offering exclusive, high-end wildlife experiences
questions.memo: Luxury private game reserves are privately run and offer exclusive services and experiences at a premium price.

questions.question: Which of these is a luxury private game reserve?
questions.memo: Sabi Sabi, like Shamwari, Madikwe and Phinda, is a luxury private game reserve.

questions.question: What does 'SANParks' stand for?
questions.memo: SANParks = South African National Parks, the body that manages the country's national parks.

questions.question: Sort each place as a NATIONAL PARK or a LUXURY PRIVATE GAME RESERVE.
questions.memo: National parks are state-run (Kruger, Addo, Table Mountain); luxury private reserves are privately owned (Shamwari, Phinda, Madikwe, Sabi Sabi).

questions.question: What is a transfrontier conservation area?
options: A large conservation area involving more than one country, working together
questions.expected: A large conservation area involving more than one country, working together
questions.memo: Transfrontier conservation areas link protected land across countries to conserve nature on a larger scale.

questions.question: The flagship national park of SANParks is the _________ National Park.
questions.memo: The Kruger National Park is SANParks' flagship.

questions.question: Which type of tourist would most likely choose a luxury private game reserve?
options: A traveller wanting exclusive service and willing to pay a premium
A backpacker on the tightest possible budget
A business traveller wanting only a city hotel
questions.expected: A traveller wanting exclusive service and willing to pay a premium
questions.memo: Luxury private reserves appeal to tourists who want exclusivity and premium experiences and can pay more.

questions.question: What is the main focus of a national park?
questions.memo: National parks exist mainly to conserve nature and wildlife, while allowing responsible tourism.

questions.question: True or false: Kirstenbosch is a national botanical garden, not a game reserve.
questions.memo: Kirstenbosch is South Africa's flagship national botanical garden, focused on indigenous plants.

questions.question: Which activity is most associated with a visit to the Kruger National Park?
questions.memo: Game drives and wildlife viewing are the main activities tourists enjoy in Kruger.

questions.question: The Ai-Ais/Richtersveld Transfrontier Park is shared between South Africa and which country?
questions.memo: The Ai-Ais/Richtersveld Transfrontier Park is shared by South Africa and Namibia.

questions.question: A reserve that crosses an international border and is co-managed by two countries is called a _________ park.
questions.memo: Transfrontier parks cross borders and are jointly managed by neighbouring countries.

questions.question: Sort each park as a SINGLE-COUNTRY national park or a TRANSFRONTIER park.
questions.memo: Transfrontier parks (Kgalagadi, Ai-Ais/Richtersveld, Greater Limpopo) cross borders; the rest sit within South Africa alone.

TOUR.G10.T3.FAUNAFLORA.A1.title: South African fauna, flora & botanical gardens
TOUR.G10.T3.FAUNAFLORA.A1.description: Concepts of biodiversity, ecosystem, species, habitat, endangered, indigenous, alien, poaching and culling in a tourism context; national botanical gardens with Kirstenbosch as the flagship.
TOUR.G10.T3.FAUNAFLORA.A1.recovery_strategy: Indigenous = naturally occurring in that place; alien = brought in from elsewhere. Endangered = at risk of dying out; extinct = already gone.

questions.question: In tourism, 'fauna' refers to:
questions.memo: Fauna means the animal life of a region; flora means the plant life.

questions.question: In tourism, 'flora' refers to:
questions.memo: Flora is the plant life of a region.

questions.question: What does 'biodiversity' mean?
options: The variety of living things (plants and animals) in an area
The number of roads in an area
questions.expected: The variety of living things (plants and animals) in an area
questions.memo: Biodiversity is the variety of life — the range of different species in a place.

questions.question: What does 'indigenous' mean?
options: Naturally occurring in a particular area
questions.expected: Naturally occurring in a particular area
questions.memo: Indigenous species occur naturally in an area; alien species are introduced from elsewhere.

questions.question: What does 'alien' (in the context of species) mean?
options: A species brought in from another area or country
A species that occurs naturally in the area
questions.expected: A species brought in from another area or country
questions.memo: Alien species are introduced from elsewhere and are not native to the area.

questions.question: What does 'endangered' mean?
options: At serious risk of dying out
questions.expected: At serious risk of dying out
questions.memo: An endangered species is at high risk of extinction; an extinct species has already died out.

questions.question: What does 'extinct' mean?
options: A species that has completely died out
A species kept on a game farm
questions.expected: A species that has completely died out
questions.memo: Extinct means no members of the species are left alive anywhere.

questions.question: What is 'poaching'?
options: Illegally hunting or capturing wild animals
questions.expected: Illegally hunting or capturing wild animals
questions.memo: Poaching is the illegal hunting or capture of wildlife, a serious threat to species like rhino.

questions.question: What is a botanical garden?
options: A garden where plants are grown, displayed and conserved, often for the public
A zoo for wild animals only
A farm that grows crops for sale
questions.expected: A garden where plants are grown, displayed and conserved, often for the public
questions.memo: Botanical gardens grow and conserve plants and let the public enjoy and learn about them.

questions.question: Which is South Africa's flagship national botanical garden?
questions.memo: Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden in Cape Town is the flagship botanical garden.

questions.question: Sort each word as referring to FAUNA or FLORA.
questions.memo: Fauna = animals; flora = plants.

questions.question: A species that occurs naturally in South Africa is described as _________.
questions.memo: Indigenous = naturally occurring in the area.

questions.question: True or false: An alien plant species is one that occurs naturally in South Africa.
questions.memo: Alien species are introduced from elsewhere; indigenous species occur naturally.

questions.question: What is a 'habitat'?
options: The natural home where a plant or animal lives
questions.expected: The natural home where a plant or animal lives
questions.memo: A habitat is the natural environment in which a species lives.

questions.question: Why do tourists visit botanical gardens such as Kirstenbosch?
options: To enjoy and learn about indigenous plants in a beautiful setting
questions.expected: To enjoy and learn about indigenous plants in a beautiful setting
questions.memo: Botanical gardens attract tourists who enjoy plants, scenery and learning about flora.

questions.question: True or false: Poaching is a threat to endangered species such as the rhino.
questions.memo: Illegal poaching pushes already-endangered species like the rhino closer to extinction.

questions.question: Sort each term as describing a species that is INDIGENOUS or ALIEN.

items.text: A foreign plant that invades local habitats

questions.memo: Indigenous = naturally belongs there; alien = brought in from elsewhere.

questions.question: A list of species at risk of extinction is known as the _________ data list.
questions.memo: The Red Data List records species that are threatened or endangered.

questions.question: Why is South Africa's rich fauna and flora important for tourism?
options: It is a major attraction that draws visitors to parks and gardens
It has no effect on tourism
questions.expected: It is a major attraction that draws visitors to parks and gardens
questions.memo: South Africa's wildlife and plant life are key draws for nature-based and eco-tourism.

questions.question: True or false: Kirstenbosch focuses mainly on growing and conserving indigenous South African plants.
questions.memo: Kirstenbosch is famous for showcasing and conserving indigenous South African flora.

TOUR.G10.T3.SUSTAIN.A1.title: Sustainable tourism — the three pillars
TOUR.G10.T3.SUSTAIN.A1.description: What sustainability means in tourism; the need for sustainable practices; the three pillars (planet/environmental, people/social, profit/economic) and the impact of tourism businesses on each.
TOUR.G10.T3.SUSTAIN.A1.recovery_strategy: Three Ps: Planet (environment), People (communities/society), Profit (economy). Ask which one an example most affects.

questions.question: What does 'sustainability' mean in tourism?
options: Meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to enjoy the same resources
Making the most money as fast as possible
Building as many hotels as possible
questions.expected: Meeting today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to enjoy the same resources
questions.memo: Sustainability means using resources responsibly now so they remain for future generations.

questions.question: What are the three pillars of sustainable tourism?
questions.memo: The three pillars are planet (environment), people (society) and profit (economy).

questions.question: The environmental ('planet') pillar is concerned with:
options: The impact of tourism on the natural environment
questions.expected: The impact of tourism on the natural environment
questions.memo: The planet pillar looks at how tourism affects nature — water, energy, wildlife and pollution.

questions.question: The social ('people') pillar is concerned with:
options: The impact of tourism on local communities and people
The amount of fuel used by aeroplanes
The number of rooms in a hotel
questions.expected: The impact of tourism on local communities and people
questions.memo: The people pillar looks at how tourism affects communities — jobs, culture and wellbeing.

questions.question: The economic ('profit') pillar is concerned with:
options: Tourism being financially viable and benefiting the local economy
questions.expected: Tourism being financially viable and benefiting the local economy
questions.memo: The profit pillar is about tourism making enough money to survive and to benefit local economies.

questions.question: True or false: Sustainable tourism ignores the needs of future generations.
questions.memo: Sustainability is all about protecting resources FOR future generations.

questions.question: The three pillars of sustainable tourism are planet, people and _________.
questions.memo: Planet, people and profit — sometimes called the 'triple bottom line'.

questions.question: Sort each example under the pillar it mainly relates to.

items.text: Earning enough income to keep the business open
Spending that supports the local economy

questions.memo: Planet = environment; people = community/society; profit = economy.

questions.question: Which is an example of an ENVIRONMENTAL (planet) sustainable practice?
options: A lodge recycling its waste and saving water
A lodge paying a dividend to shareholders
A lodge raising its room rates
questions.expected: A lodge recycling its waste and saving water
questions.memo: Recycling and saving water protect the natural environment — the planet pillar.

questions.question: Which is an example of a SOCIAL (people) sustainable practice?
options: Employing and training local community members
Switching off lights to save power
questions.expected: Employing and training local community members
questions.memo: Hiring and training local people benefits the community — the people pillar.

questions.question: Which is an example of an ECONOMIC (profit) sustainable practice?
options: Buying supplies from local businesses so money stays in the area
Letting taps run to waste water
questions.expected: Buying supplies from local businesses so money stays in the area
questions.memo: Supporting local suppliers keeps money circulating in the local economy — the profit pillar.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by selecting the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Tourism businesses should adopt sustainable practices.

pool.text: It protects the natural attractions that tourists come to see
It benefits and keeps the support of local communities
It helps the business survive and remain profitable in the long term
Sustainable hotels sometimes have green-coloured logos
Some tourists own cameras

questions.memo: The strong points connect to all three pillars — planet, people and profit. The red herrings are irrelevant details.

questions.question: True or false: Sustainable tourism tries to balance the planet, people and profit.
questions.memo: Sustainability balances all three pillars rather than focusing on just one.

questions.question: Why are sustainable practices needed in tourism?
options: Natural and cultural resources are limited and must be protected for the future
Profit is the only thing that matters
questions.expected: Natural and cultural resources are limited and must be protected for the future
questions.memo: Tourism depends on natural and cultural resources that can be damaged or used up, so they must be protected.

questions.question: The pillar concerned with the natural environment is the _________ pillar.
questions.memo: The environmental (planet) pillar deals with nature and the environment.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about sustainable tourism.

items.text: It protects resources for future generations
It balances planet, people and profit
It means using up resources as fast as possible

questions.memo: Sustainable tourism protects the future and balances all three pillars — it does not exhaust resources or ignore the environment.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three pillars of sustainable tourism?
questions.memo: The three pillars are planet, people and profit. Politics is not one of them.

questions.question: A hotel installs solar panels to generate clean energy. This mainly supports which pillar?
questions.memo: Clean energy reduces environmental harm, supporting the planet pillar (it can also save money over time).

questions.question: A lodge trains and employs people from the nearby village. This mainly supports which pillar?
questions.memo: Employing and developing local people supports the community — the people pillar.

questions.question: True or false: Making a fair profit so a business can survive long-term is part of sustainable tourism.
questions.memo: The profit pillar recognises that a business must be financially viable to keep operating and benefiting people and the planet.

TOUR.G10.T3.RESPONSIBLE.A1.title: Responsible tourism & good environmental practices
TOUR.G10.T3.RESPONSIBLE.A1.description: Responsible tourist behaviour towards the environment and host communities; the negative impacts of tourism; rules for behaviour in nature; and good environmental practices (litter control, conserving energy and water) and their benefits.
TOUR.G10.T3.RESPONSIBLE.A1.recovery_strategy: Sustainable tourism is the GOAL (lasting balance of planet/people/profit); responsible tourism is the BEHAVIOUR of tourists and businesses that helps reach it.

questions.question: What is responsible tourism?
options: Travelling in a way that minimises harm to the environment and host communities
Travelling as cheaply as possible whatever the cost to others
Visiting as many countries as possible
questions.expected: Travelling in a way that minimises harm to the environment and host communities
questions.memo: Responsible tourism is behaviour that reduces negative impacts on nature and local people.

questions.question: How do sustainable tourism and responsible tourism differ?
options: Sustainability is the goal; responsible behaviour is how tourists and businesses help reach it
questions.expected: Sustainability is the goal; responsible behaviour is how tourists and businesses help reach it
questions.memo: Sustainability is the aim (lasting balance of planet/people/profit); responsible tourism is the behaviour that achieves it.

questions.question: Which is an example of responsible tourist behaviour?
options: Taking your litter with you and staying on marked paths
questions.expected: Taking your litter with you and staying on marked paths
questions.memo: Responsible tourists protect nature — they remove litter and keep to paths to avoid damage.

questions.question: Which is a negative impact of tourism on the natural environment?
options: Litter, pollution and damage to habitats
questions.expected: Litter, pollution and damage to habitats
questions.memo: Poorly managed tourism can cause litter, pollution and harm to natural habitats.

questions.question: Which is a negative impact of tourism on a host community?
questions.memo: Too much or poorly managed tourism can overcrowd a place and push up prices for local residents.

questions.question: True or false: Leaving litter behind in a national park is responsible behaviour.
questions.memo: Littering harms the environment and wildlife — it is irresponsible behaviour.

questions.question: Conserving energy and water are examples of good _________ practices.
questions.memo: Saving energy and water are good environmental practices.

questions.question: Sort each action as RESPONSIBLE or IRRESPONSIBLE tourist behaviour.

items.text: Using bins and recycling where provided
Carving your name into a rock
Feeding wild monkeys at a viewpoint
Leaving taps running in your room

questions.memo: Responsible behaviour protects nature and people; irresponsible behaviour damages the environment or disrespects communities.

questions.question: Which is a good rule for tourist behaviour in a natural environment?
options: Do not feed or disturb wild animals
Pick as many plants as you like
Leave fires burning when you go
questions.expected: Do not feed or disturb wild animals
questions.memo: Not feeding or disturbing wildlife keeps animals wild, healthy and safe.

questions.question: What is a benefit of litter control as a good environmental practice?
options: It keeps attractions clean and protects wildlife
questions.expected: It keeps attractions clean and protects wildlife
questions.memo: Controlling litter keeps places attractive and safe for wildlife, which is good for tourism too.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by selecting the strong points.
questions.thesis: Tourists should behave responsibly in natural areas.

pool.text: It protects wildlife and habitats from harm
It keeps attractions beautiful so future visitors can enjoy them
It shows respect for local communities and their resources
Natural areas often have nice views for photographs
Some tourists wear hats

questions.memo: The strong points explain how responsible behaviour protects nature, attractions and communities. The red herrings are irrelevant.

questions.question: True or false: Good environmental practices benefit the tourism industry in the long run.
questions.memo: Protecting the environment keeps the attractions that draw tourists, helping the industry survive long-term.

questions.question: Compare these two accounts of tourist behaviour, then judge each statement.

source_a.text: Our group stuck to the marked trails, took all our litter back to camp, and kept a respectful distance from the elephants while watching them.
source_a.provenance: Tourist's travel blog about a guided walk

source_b.text: We drove off the road to get closer for photos, fed some of the monkeys our leftover chips, and left our wrappers at the viewpoint.

statements.text: Describes behaviour that harms the environment and wildlife

questions.memo: Source A shows responsible behaviour (trails, litter removal, distance); Source B shows irresponsible behaviour (off-road, feeding animals, littering). Both visit nature; neither mentions a fee.

questions.question: What is a benefit of good environmental practices FOR THE TOURISM INDUSTRY?
options: Attractions stay clean and appealing, so tourists keep coming
It has no effect on visitor numbers
questions.expected: Attractions stay clean and appealing, so tourists keep coming
questions.memo: Well-kept, clean attractions remain appealing, which keeps drawing tourists and protects the industry.

questions.question: A tourist who respects the environment and the host community is a _________ tourist.
questions.memo: Such behaviour defines a responsible tourist.

questions.question: Which action helps reduce water use at a hotel?
options: Reusing towels instead of having them washed daily
Filling the pool twice a day
Hosing down the car park hourly
questions.expected: Reusing towels instead of having them washed daily
questions.memo: Reusing towels reduces laundry and saves water — a simple responsible practice.

questions.question: Sort each practice as GOOD or POOR for the environment.

items.text: Switching off lights not in use

questions.memo: Good practices conserve resources and reduce pollution; poor practices waste resources and pollute.

questions.question: True or false: Feeding wild animals at attractions is recommended responsible behaviour.
questions.memo: Feeding wild animals harms their health and natural behaviour, so it is irresponsible.

questions.question: Why should tourists follow the rules in a natural environment?
options: To protect wildlife, habitats and other visitors' enjoyment
To make their visit as harmful as possible
questions.expected: To protect wildlife, habitats and other visitors' enjoyment
questions.memo: Rules exist to safeguard nature and ensure everyone can enjoy the area now and in future.

questions.question: Which is an example of conserving a scarce resource while travelling?
options: Taking shorter showers to save water
Leaving the air conditioner on all day in an empty room
Printing documents you do not need
questions.expected: Taking shorter showers to save water
questions.memo: Shorter showers conserve water, a scarce resource — a responsible, good environmental practice.

TOUR.G10.T3.GLOBALWARM.A1.title: Global warming & the tourism industry
TOUR.G10.T3.GLOBALWARM.A1.description: The concepts of global warming and carbon footprint; causes of global warming; consequences of climate change for tourism; and how establishments and tourists can reduce their carbon footprint.
TOUR.G10.T3.GLOBALWARM.A1.recovery_strategy: A carbon footprint measures greenhouse gases released by an activity. The biggest tourism contributors are transport (especially flights) and energy use.

questions.question: What is global warming?
options: The gradual rise in the Earth's average temperature
The cooling of the Earth's oceans
questions.expected: The gradual rise in the Earth's average temperature
questions.memo: Global warming is the long-term rise in the Earth's average temperature, driven largely by greenhouse gases.

questions.question: What is a 'carbon footprint'?
options: The amount of greenhouse gases produced by an activity
A footprint left in the sand
The number of tourists at a site
questions.expected: The amount of greenhouse gases produced by an activity
questions.memo: A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases (like carbon dioxide) released by an activity, person or business.

questions.question: What is a major cause of global warming?
options: Greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels
questions.expected: Greenhouse gases released by burning fossil fuels
questions.memo: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, petrol) releases greenhouse gases that trap heat and warm the planet.

questions.question: Which is a consequence of climate change for the tourism industry?
options: Extreme weather and rising seas can damage attractions and beaches
questions.expected: Extreme weather and rising seas can damage attractions and beaches
questions.memo: Climate change brings extreme weather, rising seas and shifting seasons that can harm the attractions tourism depends on.

questions.question: How can an accommodation establishment reduce its carbon footprint?
options: Use solar power and energy-efficient lighting
Leave all lights and air conditioners on overnight
Waste as much water as possible
questions.expected: Use solar power and energy-efficient lighting
questions.memo: Clean energy and efficient lighting cut the greenhouse gases an establishment produces.

questions.question: How can a tourist reduce their own carbon footprint?
options: Use public transport and take fewer unnecessary flights
Fly as often as possible for short trips
Leave hotel lights on all day
Use a private car for every short trip
questions.expected: Use public transport and take fewer unnecessary flights
questions.memo: Choosing public transport and limiting flights cuts a tourist's greenhouse-gas emissions.

questions.question: True or false: Air travel generally produces a large carbon footprint.
questions.memo: Flying burns large amounts of fuel, making it one of the biggest contributors to a traveller's carbon footprint.

questions.question: The amount of greenhouse gas an activity produces is called its carbon _________.
questions.memo: Carbon footprint = the greenhouse gases released by an activity.

questions.question: Sort each action as one that INCREASES or REDUCES a carbon footprint.

items.text: Using a train or bus instead of flying
Leaving air conditioners running all day

questions.memo: Burning more fossil fuel raises the footprint; clean energy and efficient transport lower it.

questions.question: Which mode of transport generally has the LARGEST carbon footprint per passenger over a similar trip?
questions.memo: Flying burns the most fuel per passenger; buses, bicycles and walking have much smaller footprints.

questions.question: True or false: Global warming means the Earth is gradually cooling down.
questions.memo: Global WARMING means the Earth's average temperature is RISING, not falling.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by selecting the strong points.
questions.thesis: The tourism industry should work to reduce its carbon footprint.

pool.text: Climate change damages the natural attractions tourism relies on
Cutting energy use also saves businesses money
Many tourists now prefer eco-friendly, responsible businesses
Aeroplanes can be very large
Some hotels have swimming pools

questions.memo: Strong points link reducing emissions to protecting attractions, saving money and meeting customer demand. The red herrings are irrelevant facts.

questions.question: How might climate change affect a coastal beach destination?
options: Rising sea levels and storms can erode beaches and damage facilities
questions.expected: Rising sea levels and storms can erode beaches and damage facilities
questions.memo: Higher seas and stronger storms can wash away beaches and damage the resorts that depend on them.

questions.question: Global warming is the rise in the Earth's average _________.
questions.memo: Global warming refers to the rising average temperature of the Earth.

questions.question: Which action at a guesthouse helps reduce its carbon footprint?
options: Fitting energy-saving LED lights and recycling waste
Throwing all recyclables in one bin to landfill
Watering the garden during the hottest hours daily
questions.expected: Fitting energy-saving LED lights and recycling waste
questions.memo: Energy-saving lighting and recycling cut emissions and waste.

questions.question: Sort each measure as something a HOTEL can do or something a TOURIST can do to cut emissions.

items.text: Choose to travel by bus instead of flying
Fit occupancy sensors to switch off lights
Reuse a towel rather than getting a fresh one daily

questions.memo: Hotels control building systems (solar, sensors, appliances); tourists control their own choices (transport, towel reuse).

questions.question: True or false: Using public transport instead of a private car can lower a tourist's carbon footprint.
questions.memo: Sharing transport spreads emissions over more people, lowering each traveller's footprint.

questions.question: Why should the tourism industry care about global warming?
options: Tourism depends on a healthy climate and natural attractions
Global warming makes no difference to tourism
questions.expected: Tourism depends on a healthy climate and natural attractions
questions.memo: Many attractions (beaches, parks, wildlife) depend on a stable climate, so global warming directly threatens tourism.

questions.question: Which is a source of greenhouse gases linked to tourism?
options: Burning fuel in aeroplanes and vehicles
questions.expected: Burning fuel in aeroplanes and vehicles
questions.memo: Transport fuel is a major source of tourism's greenhouse-gas emissions.

questions.question: True or false: Planting trees can help offset (cancel out) some carbon emissions.
questions.memo: Trees absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, so planting them can help offset some emissions.

TOUR.G10.T3.MARKETING.A1.title: Marketing of tourism products, services & sites
TOUR.G10.T3.MARKETING.A1.description: Marketing concepts (market research, target market, market share, competitive edge, niche market); the purpose of marketing; the market-research process and the marketing mix (the five Ps: product, promotion, price, place, people).
TOUR.G10.T3.MARKETING.A1.recovery_strategy: Target market = the GROUP you aim a product at. Market share = the PORTION of total sales a business holds. The five Ps are product, promotion, price, place, people.

questions.question: What is marketing in tourism?
options: The activities used to promote and sell tourism products and services to customers
questions.expected: The activities used to promote and sell tourism products and services to customers
questions.memo: Marketing covers everything done to make customers aware of, and want to buy, a product or service.

questions.question: What is a 'target market'?
options: The specific group of customers a product is aimed at
The total sales of all businesses
The place where products are made
questions.expected: The specific group of customers a product is aimed at
questions.memo: A target market is the group of people a business designs and aims its product at.

questions.question: What is 'market share'?
options: The portion of total sales in a market that one business holds
The group a product is aimed at
The number of staff a business employs
questions.expected: The portion of total sales in a market that one business holds
questions.memo: Market share is the slice of all sales in a market that belongs to one business.

questions.question: What is 'market research'?
options: Gathering information about customers and the market
questions.expected: Gathering information about customers and the market
questions.memo: Market research collects information about customers, competitors and trends to guide decisions.

questions.question: What is a 'niche market'?
options: A small, specialised group of customers with particular interests
The entire population of a country
questions.expected: A small, specialised group of customers with particular interests
questions.memo: A niche market is a small, focused segment — for example bird-watching or luxury wine tours.

questions.question: What is a 'competitive edge'?
options: An advantage that makes a business stand out from its competitors
questions.expected: An advantage that makes a business stand out from its competitors
questions.memo: A competitive edge is something that makes a business more attractive than its rivals, such as a unique experience or better price.

questions.question: The five Ps of the marketing mix are product, promotion, price, place and _________.
questions.memo: The five Ps are product, promotion, price, place and people.

questions.question: Match each 'P' of the marketing mix to its meaning.

items.text: What is being sold (the tour, room or service)
The cost charged for the offering
The actual experience or item offered

questions.memo: Product = what is sold; price = what it costs; promotion = how it is advertised.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of marketing tourism products and services?
options: To attract customers and persuade them to buy
To hide the product from customers
To reduce the number of visitors
questions.expected: To attract customers and persuade them to buy
questions.memo: Marketing aims to make people aware of a product and persuade them to choose and buy it.

questions.question: True or false: Market research helps a business understand what its customers want.
questions.memo: Research reveals customers' needs and preferences, helping the business offer the right product.

questions.question: In the marketing mix, 'product' refers to:
options: The tour, service or experience that is being offered
questions.expected: The tour, service or experience that is being offered
questions.memo: Product is what the business actually offers — a tour, room, meal or experience.

questions.question: In the marketing mix, 'price' refers to:
options: How much the customer pays for the product
questions.expected: How much the customer pays for the product
questions.memo: Price is the amount charged to the customer.

questions.question: In the marketing mix, 'place' refers to:
options: Where and how the product is made available to customers
questions.expected: Where and how the product is made available to customers
questions.memo: Place is about how customers can access or buy the product — online, through agents, or in person.

questions.question: In the marketing mix, 'promotion' refers to:
options: Advertising and communicating the product to customers
The location of the head office
questions.expected: Advertising and communicating the product to customers
questions.memo: Promotion covers advertising and all communication used to make customers aware and interested.

questions.question: A business's portion of total sales in a market is its market _________.
questions.memo: Market share = the portion of total market sales a business holds.

questions.question: True or false: A target market is always the entire population of a country.
questions.memo: A target market is a specific group, not everyone — for example families, adventure travellers or luxury tourists.

questions.question: Sort each description under the correct 'P' of the marketing mix.

items.text: Selling tours through a website and travel agents
Friendly, well-trained staff who serve customers

questions.memo: Place = where/how it is sold; people = the staff who deliver it; promotion = how it is advertised.

questions.question: Which is an example of a niche tourism market?
options: Anyone who travels for any reason
The whole population of a city
questions.memo: Bird-watching tours target a small, specialised group — a niche market.

questions.question: Why should a business do market research BEFORE launching a new tourism product?
options: To check there is demand and design the product to suit customers
To make sure nobody hears about the product
To avoid learning anything about customers
questions.expected: To check there is demand and design the product to suit customers
questions.memo: Research reduces risk by confirming demand and shaping the product to what customers actually want.

questions.question: Which is an example of a competitive edge for a tour operator?
options: Offering a unique experience that rivals cannot match
Charging far more for exactly the same product
questions.expected: Offering a unique experience that rivals cannot match
questions.memo: A competitive edge sets a business apart — for example a unique tour, better value or special service.

TOUR.G10.T4.CULTURE.A1.title: Culture & heritage — concepts and elements
TOUR.G10.T4.CULTURE.A1.description: The concepts culture, heritage and cultural diversity; elements of culture (architecture, interiors, arts and crafts, cuisine, music and dance); and the importance of conserving heritage for future generations.
TOUR.G10.T4.CULTURE.A1.recovery_strategy: Culture = a group's shared way of life NOW (food, music, dress). Heritage = what is INHERITED from the past and worth conserving for the future.

questions.question: What is 'culture'?
options: A group of people's shared way of life — their customs, food, language and beliefs
Only the money a country has
questions.expected: A group of people's shared way of life — their customs, food, language and beliefs
questions.memo: Culture is the shared way of life of a group, including customs, food, language, art and beliefs.

questions.question: What is 'heritage'?
options: What is inherited from the past and passed on to future generations
questions.expected: What is inherited from the past and passed on to future generations
questions.memo: Heritage is what we inherit from the past — traditions, buildings and places worth conserving for the future.

questions.question: What does 'cultural diversity' mean?
options: The variety of different cultures within a society
Everyone having exactly the same culture
questions.expected: The variety of different cultures within a society
questions.memo: Cultural diversity is the presence of many different cultures — a key feature of South Africa.

questions.question: Which of these is an ELEMENT of culture?
questions.memo: Elements of culture include architecture, arts and crafts, cuisine, music and dance.

questions.question: Why is it important to conserve heritage?
options: So that future generations can learn from and enjoy it
questions.expected: So that future generations can learn from and enjoy it
questions.memo: Conserving heritage keeps a society's history and identity alive for future generations.

questions.question: True or false: Culture and heritage mean exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: Culture is a group's present way of life; heritage is what is inherited from the past. They are related but not the same.

questions.question: A culture's food and cooking style is an element of culture known as _________.
questions.memo: Cuisine — the food and cooking traditions of a group — is an element of culture.

questions.question: Sort each item as an ELEMENT OF CULTURE or NOT an element of culture.

items.text: The exchange rate of the rand

questions.memo: Elements of culture include music, dance, cuisine, architecture and crafts. Exchange rates and distance tables are not cultural elements.

questions.question: Traditional dance performed at a cultural village is an element of culture relating to:
questions.memo: Dance falls under the 'music and dance' element of culture.

questions.question: Which is an example of South Africa's cultural diversity?
options: Many languages, traditions and cuisines living side by side
A single style of music for the whole country
One identical tradition shared by all
questions.expected: Many languages, traditions and cuisines living side by side
questions.memo: South Africa's many languages and traditions are a clear example of cultural diversity — a tourism drawcard.

questions.question: True or false: Heritage is something inherited from the past.
questions.memo: Heritage is what is passed down from earlier generations.

questions.question: A group of people's shared way of life is called their _________.
questions.memo: Culture = a group's shared way of life.

questions.question: Match each cultural element to an example.
questions.memo: Architecture = building styles; cuisine = food; music and dance = performance traditions.

questions.question: Handmade beadwork and pottery are an element of culture known as:
questions.memo: Beadwork and pottery are examples of arts and crafts, an element of culture.

questions.question: Why is cultural diversity valuable for tourism?
options: Variety of cultures gives tourists rich and interesting experiences
It makes all places look the same
It has no link to tourism
questions.expected: Variety of cultures gives tourists rich and interesting experiences
questions.memo: A diverse mix of cultures gives tourists more to see and experience, strengthening a destination's appeal.

questions.question: True or false: Conserving heritage benefits future generations.
questions.memo: Conserving heritage means future generations can still experience and learn from it.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an element of culture?
questions.memo: Cuisine, music and architecture are cultural elements; the exchange rate is an economic figure, not a cultural element.

questions.question: Sort each item as part of present CULTURE or as HERITAGE from the past.

items.text: A traditional building inherited from past generations

questions.memo: Culture is the living way of life now; heritage is what has been inherited from the past.

questions.question: Which is an example of a South African cultural element a tourist might experience?
options: Tasting traditional dishes and watching local dance
questions.expected: Tasting traditional dishes and watching local dance
questions.memo: Cuisine and dance are cultural experiences tourists can enjoy.

questions.question: What is the main importance of conserving a country's heritage?
options: It preserves history and identity and can attract cultural tourists
It wastes money for no reason
It stops a country from developing
It has no benefits at all
questions.expected: It preserves history and identity and can attract cultural tourists
questions.memo: Conserving heritage protects a nation's history and identity and is itself a draw for cultural tourism.

TOUR.G10.T4.HERITSITES.A1.title: Heritage sites in South Africa
TOUR.G10.T4.HERITSITES.A1.description: Cultural heritage sites (monuments, museums, historical buildings, graveyards) and natural heritage sites (mountains, waterfalls, caves); the difference between local, provincial and national heritage sites; and the heritage plaque that marks a national site.
TOUR.G10.T4.HERITSITES.A1.recovery_strategy: Cultural heritage = made or shaped by PEOPLE (monuments, buildings). Natural heritage = formed by NATURE (mountains, caves, waterfalls).

questions.question: Which is an example of a CULTURAL heritage site?
questions.memo: Cultural heritage sites are made or shaped by people — monuments, museums and historic buildings.

questions.question: Which is an example of a NATURAL heritage site?
questions.memo: Natural heritage sites are formed by nature — mountains, waterfalls and caves.

questions.question: What is the difference between a cultural and a natural heritage site?
options: Cultural sites are made or shaped by people; natural sites are formed by nature
Cultural sites are formed by nature; natural sites are built by people
questions.expected: Cultural sites are made or shaped by people; natural sites are formed by nature
questions.memo: People create cultural heritage (monuments, buildings); nature creates natural heritage (mountains, caves).

questions.question: Heritage sites in South Africa can be classified as local, provincial or _________.
questions.memo: Heritage sites are graded by significance: local, provincial or national.

questions.question: True or false: A waterfall is best classified as a cultural heritage site.
questions.memo: A waterfall is formed by nature, so it is a natural heritage site.

questions.question: A site declared nationally important is identified by a heritage _________.
questions.memo: A heritage plaque marks a site that has been declared a national heritage site.

questions.question: Sort each site as CULTURAL or NATURAL heritage.
questions.memo: Made by people = cultural; formed by nature = natural.

questions.question: A museum is best classified as which type of heritage site?
questions.memo: A museum, made and run by people, is a cultural heritage site.

questions.question: A system of natural caves is best classified as which type of heritage site?
questions.memo: Caves are natural features, so they are natural heritage sites.

questions.question: True or false: Monuments and historic buildings are cultural heritage sites.
questions.memo: Monuments and historic buildings are made by people, so they are cultural heritage.

questions.question: Which body is responsible for South Africa's heritage resources?
options: The South African Heritage Resources Agency (SAHRA)
questions.expected: The South African Heritage Resources Agency (SAHRA)
questions.memo: SAHRA manages and protects South Africa's heritage resources.

questions.question: Monuments, museums and historic buildings are examples of _________ heritage sites.
questions.memo: These are all human-made, so they are cultural heritage sites.

questions.question: Sort each heritage site by its likely level of significance.

items.text: A small monument important mainly to one town
A site of importance to the whole country, with a national plaque
A neighbourhood historic house known locally

questions.memo: Local sites matter mainly to a community; national sites are significant to the whole country and are nationally declared.

questions.question: Why is it important to conserve heritage sites?
options: To preserve history and identity and attract cultural tourists
To stop people learning about the past
questions.expected: To preserve history and identity and attract cultural tourists
questions.memo: Conserving heritage sites keeps history alive and draws cultural and heritage tourists.

questions.question: True or false: A national heritage site is generally of greater significance than a local one.
questions.memo: National heritage sites are significant to the whole country, ranking above provincial and local sites.

questions.question: Which is an example of a natural heritage site in South Africa?
questions.memo: The Cango Caves are a natural feature; the others are human-made cultural heritage sites.

questions.question: Sort each example as CULTURAL or NATURAL heritage.

items.text: An old graveyard of historical importance

questions.memo: Human-made or human-significant objects and buildings are cultural; landforms are natural.

questions.question: An old graveyard and a historic building are best classified as:
questions.memo: Graveyards and historic buildings are human-made, so they are cultural heritage.

questions.question: What does a heritage plaque on a building tell visitors?
options: That the site has been declared a heritage site worth protecting
That the building is for sale
questions.expected: That the site has been declared a heritage site worth protecting
questions.memo: A heritage plaque marks a site that has been officially declared and protected for its heritage value.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a LOCAL and a NATIONAL heritage site?
options: A national site is significant to the whole country; a local site mainly to its community
A local site is always larger than a national one
National sites are always natural and local ones always cultural
questions.expected: A national site is significant to the whole country; a local site mainly to its community
questions.memo: The difference is the level of significance — national sites matter countrywide; local sites matter mainly to their community.

TOUR.G10.T4.COMMS.A1.title: Communication & communication technology
TOUR.G10.T4.COMMS.A1.description: Equipment used to communicate in a tourism business (landlines, cellphones, fax, photocopiers, printers, computers with email, video- and teleconferencing) and their functions, advantages and disadvantages; verbal and written communication including email netiquette and tourism road/information signs.
TOUR.G10.T4.COMMS.A1.recovery_strategy: Verbal = SPOKEN (face-to-face, phone). Written = recorded in TEXT (email, SMS, memo, fax). Netiquette = good manners when communicating online.

questions.question: Which of these is a piece of communication technology used in a tourism business?
questions.memo: Communication technology includes computers (with email), telephones, cellphones, fax machines, printers and photocopiers.

questions.question: What is VERBAL communication?
questions.memo: Verbal communication is spoken — face-to-face or by phone.

questions.question: Which is an example of WRITTEN communication?
questions.memo: Written communication is recorded in text — emails, SMSes, memos and faxes.

questions.question: What is 'email netiquette'?
options: Good manners and polite behaviour when communicating by email
questions.expected: Good manners and polite behaviour when communicating by email
questions.memo: Netiquette is polite, professional conduct when communicating online, including in emails.

questions.question: True or false: An email is a form of written communication.
questions.memo: Email is text-based, so it is written communication.

questions.question: Polite, professional behaviour when sending emails is called email _________.
questions.memo: Email netiquette = good online manners.

questions.question: Sort each example as VERBAL or WRITTEN communication.

items.text: A telephone call to a guest

questions.memo: Spoken = verbal (calls, conversations, commentary); text-based = written (email, SMS, memo).

questions.question: What is an advantage of using email in a tourism business?
options: It is fast, low-cost and keeps a written record
questions.expected: It is fast, low-cost and keeps a written record
questions.memo: Email is quick and cheap and leaves a written record that can be referred to later.

questions.question: What is video-conferencing mainly used for?
options: Holding meetings with people in different places using live video
questions.expected: Holding meetings with people in different places using live video
questions.memo: Video-conferencing lets people in different locations meet live by video, saving travel time and cost.

questions.question: Tourism road and information signs are a form of:
options: Communication that guides and informs travellers
questions.expected: Communication that guides and informs travellers
questions.memo: Road and tourism information signs communicate directions and information to travellers.

questions.question: True or false: A fax machine sends copies of documents over telephone lines.
questions.memo: A fax machine transmits copies of documents over phone lines.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of relying on a fax machine today?
options: It is slower and less used than email, and needs a phone line
It is faster than every other method
It keeps no record at all
